The table is the quota of Phase 2b (the quota of Phase 2a allowed 12 claims and 120Gi and counted a user scheduler, which the workbench no longer runs in the zone). A fifth notebook server that would cross the quota does not start: the hub shows the cluster's "exceeded quota" refusal. Simulation and agent Jobs (Phase 4 on) widen the quota with rows of their own. The health check Research network policies (rsnetpol) compares every NetworkPolicy of the research namespace with the compile, specification included: OK "3 research NetworkPolicies, the compiled set (default deny included)" (the count is the compile's); FAIL when a compiled one is missing or differs, when a labelled one is no longer compiled, and when a policy without the label is there at all, since policies add up and any other one opens the zone past its default deny; SKIP while the sandbox is switched off and has no namespace, and while the applied policy has no research zone; WARN when switched off with the namespace left, when switched on without it, and when something cannot be read.

A second namespace, <NAMESPACE>-research-gw, for the gateway to the hosted model, is created with its first pod in Phase 4, not now. ./deploy-infra.sh --reset and --uninstall remove the research namespace (only one labelled medcea/zone=research), with every volume in it, and the PriorityClass, and warn about the research database's volume before they ask.

The research database

./apps/research/deploy.sh (./deploy-apps.sh --all runs it; ./medcea.sh → Applications → Install the research database) installs the research sandbox's own PostgreSQL, Helm release research-postgresql (Bitnami chart 18.4.0, the platform's version) in the research namespace, at the low priority, with its volume data-research-postgresql-0 (RESEARCH_DB_STORAGE, default 10Gi). It never touches the platform's database server. It skips with one line and exit 0 while RESEARCH_ENABLED is not true, while the applied access policy has no research zone, while no policy version is applied, and while the research namespace does not exist yet; a research database already installed is left running by a skip.

The chart's own NetworkPolicy is switched off: it would have opened port 5432 to the whole cluster. After the install the deploy stops if any NetworkPolicy in the research namespace lacks the label medcea/rs-netpol=true, naming it.

The database is medcea_research. Its roles live in the research server only:

RoleLoginWhat it may doUsed by
rs_ownernoOwns the database, its schemas and everything in themThe deploy and reserve.sh, through the server's superuser
rs_export_writeryesINSERT on the ten staging tables lake.stage_*; EXECUTE on lake.close_snapshot and lake.latest_cut; nothing elseThe nightly export (Secret research-export-writer in the platform namespace)
rs_backupyesReads everything (pg_read_all_data)The nightly backup (Secret research-backup in the platform namespace)

The schemas: lake (the snapshots), vault (the held-out reservations), and sim, agent_trace and registry, created empty for later phases. The lake and the vault are append-only: triggers refuse UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on every lake table and on vault.reservation ("… is append-only: … refused"), for rs_owner too, and they are ENABLE ALWAYS, so a replication session does not bypass them. Only the staging tables are emptied, by lake.close_snapshot itself. A superuser can still disable a trigger; no database can prevent that.

Outside the platform's access policy. The research database is not in the policy matrix and nobody signs in to it as a person. Its grants are written by hand in apps/research/db/grants.sql, and every deploy ends by checking them from the catalog (apps/research/db/assert_grants.sql): rs_export_writer holds exactly what the table above says and owns nothing, rs_backup is a member of pg_read_all_data only, PUBLIC holds nothing, and rs_owner cannot log in and owns everything. Any difference stops the deploy and lists it. The passwords (RESEARCH_DB_PASS for the server's superuser, RS_EXPORT_WRITER_DB_PASS, RS_BACKUP_DB_PASS) are generated by infra/configure.sh, never asked or shown, and reach PostgreSQL only as SCRAM verifiers.

Backup. The nightly backup dumps medcea_research from the research server as rs_backup, next to the platform's databases, whenever Secret research-backup exists and the database answers; without it its MANIFEST says the database was skipped, and a research server that does not answer is no failure of the platform's backup. A backup deployed from this code needs no redeploy when research is switched on later (it always knows the research server's address); the enable recipe runs ./apps/backup/deploy.sh anyway.

Removing it. ./apps/research/uninstall.sh removes the two Secrets and the release and keeps the volume, so a later deploy finds the same snapshots and reservations. ./apps/research/uninstall.sh --purge-data also deletes the volume: every snapshot and every reservation is gone. ./deploy-apps.sh --uninstall --purge-data never purges it; that is this script's own flag.

Held-out reservations

A reservation keeps one unit's measurements, or one zone's, with a measurement time in [from, to) out of every snapshot from then on, so a model can later be judged on data it never saw (the final validation, RS.8). Only a qa person reserves, through a command on the host:

./apps/research/reserve.sh add --by <your qa username> --unit <UNIT> [--zone <ZONE>] --from <TIME> --to <TIME> --reason "<why, 10+ characters>"
./apps/research/reserve.sh list
  • --by names the qa person making it, as their account in the platform's realm: it must exist, be enabled and hold the role qa, else "--by … does not hold the realm role qa: only qa reserves held-out data." Its username and account id are recorded with the reason.
  • TIME is ISO 8601, such as 2026-12-01 or 2026-12-01T06:00, in UTC unless it carries an offset. Without --zone every zone of the unit is held out.
  • add shows what it will hold out, says "This cannot be changed or removed afterwards." and asks for a typed yes; it takes the deploy lock. On success: "Reservation #N made: unit … [from, to) is held out of every snapshot from now on". list is read-only: "No reservations: nothing is held out of the research lake.", or a table ID, UNIT, ZONE, FROM, TO, BY, MADE, REASON (ZONE * = every zone).
  • Before the first export that would carry the data. The research database refuses a range whose measurements are already in the lake: "reserve: unit … is already exported: it is no longer held out". It also refuses a range that ends more than a year from now and a reason shorter than 10 characters. A reservation is never changed or removed.

A reservation is not an account decision and is not on the policy history: it is a row of vault.reservation in the research database (who, when, why), written as rs_owner through vault.reserve, outside the policy matrix. In ./medcea.sh: Applications → Reserve a held-out range (qa), and List the held-out reservations. The snapshot export holds a reservation out from the moment it is made; live reads by the scientists end only at the Phase 2b switchover (decision record, 17 November 2026). From Phase 2b a notebook sees which ranges are held out (unit, zone, from, to), never who made a reservation or why (Reading snapshots from a notebook).

The nightly export

./apps/research-export/deploy.sh (./medcea.sh → Applications → Install the nightly research export) installs CronJob research-export in the platform namespace: daily at 03:00 UTC, after the nightly backup, one run at a time, in the image the research database runs (so its psql matches), with no service account token and a read-only root file system. It skips like the research database, and also until that database is installed and while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is not true; it never falls back to the platform's superuser. One run:

  1. Asks the research database for the latest cut (lake.latest_cut(), none before the first snapshot).
  2. Takes the new cut from the operational database: its clock minus two minutes, so a reading whose transaction started before the cut has committed. It is refused when the cut is not after the latest one.
  3. In one read-only, repeatable-read transaction on the operational database, as svc_research_export, reads every medcea.research_*() function: the measurements ingested in (previous cut, cut], the small sets whole.
  4. In one transaction on the research database, as rs_export_writer, stages the rows and calls lake.close_snapshot, which drops every row inside a reservation, digests the rest, records the snapshot and moves the rows into the lake. Any error rolls back the whole of it: nothing is half written.
  5. Prints "research-export: snapshot N cut … measurements M", where M counts the rows read, before the reservations removed theirs.

Run one at once with microk8s kubectl -n medcea create job --from=cronjob/research-export research-export-now-1; ./apps/research-export/uninstall.sh removes the CronJob, and the snapshots stay.

What the export reads, and never reads

Migration 013 creates eleven read functions in the operational database, owned by the database owner role, each with a fixed list of columns. The exporter's login may only execute them (owner decision F): it is refused on every table. They are created inert, executable by nobody, until the skeleton version names them in the access policy for svc_research_export alone.

FunctionReturns
research_contract_version()1
research_measurements(after, upto)The AP readings ingested in (after, upto]: ingest time, measurement time, unit code, zone code, tag, sensor, value (a number, else empty), unit of measure
research_units()Unit code, recipe type, area, height, active
research_zones()Unit code, zone code, active
research_recipes()The approved and retired recipes (never a draft): id, recipe type, status
research_recipe_lines()Their lines: recipe id, sequence, cycle number, light type, light on and off minutes, setpoints
research_runs()Run id, recipe id, unit code, start, end, status
research_cycles()Every cycle: run id, sequence, cycle number, start, end, status, the controller code, its parameters and the loop map, taken out of the run's parameters
research_control_loops()The active loops: unit code, zone code, loop code, input, output
research_param_sets()The approved parameter sets: id, controller code, unit code (empty: any unit), parameters
research_catalogue()The quantity catalogue as rows: quantities, recipe types and the quantities each type requires

No person, not even a pseudonym (owner decision P). No function returns who created, changed, executed or approved anything, no account id, no name, description, note or reason, no location, no device identifier, address or serial, and no message's raw JSON. Where a result carries JSON it is rebuilt from known keys, never passed on: a parameter set keeps only keys whose value is a number or true/false, and a loop's input and output keep only the fields the runner's loop rules read, each checked for its shape (a name, a command, a number). Anything else is dropped, so nothing a person typed reaches the lake.

Snapshots and their digests

The lake is append-only and a snapshot is a high-water mark (owner decision S). Each export adds one row to lake.snapshot: snapshot_id, cut_at (the cut), previous_cut_at, created_at, contract_version, rows and digests. The measurements accumulate, each snapshot adding those ingested since the previous cut; the small sets (units, zones, recipes, recipe lines, runs, cycles, control loops, parameter sets, catalogue) are copied whole into every snapshot, each row tagged with its snapshot_id. close_snapshot refuses a contract version it does not know, a previous cut that is not the latest snapshot's (another export ran in between), a cut not after it, and a staged measurement outside (previous cut, cut].

  • rows: per set, its row count, plus held_out, the staged measurements a reservation kept out.
  • digests: per set, a sha256. For a small set it is the sha256 of its rows' text forms (under time zone UTC and ISO dates, sorted bytewise) joined with newlines.
  • For the measurements it is computed per hour of ingest time, so no step holds more than an hour of rows: for each hour that has rows, oldest first, the line <hour as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:00:00Z>|<rows in that hour>|<sha256 of that hour's sorted row texts joined with newlines>; the digest is the sha256 of those lines joined with newlines. A set with no rows digests the empty string.

The health check Research export (rsexport) reads the newest snapshot read-only: OK while it is at most 26 hours old (for example "newest snapshot 1 h old (snapshot 12, no reserved rows in it);2 reservation(s)"), WARN beyond, FAIL beyond 72 hours, as for backups; FAIL when rows of it fall in a held-out reservation ("… held-out data reached the lake"); WARN while there is no reservation ("no reservation yet: nothing is held out for validation …") and when something cannot be read; SKIP without the CronJob and, with no snapshot yet, during the CronJob's first 26 hours. With Research network policies it brings the health check from 66 to 68 checks.

The order to switch it on, once the skeleton version with the research zone is applied, is what the RESEARCH_ENABLED enable recipe of ./medcea.sh runs: set RESEARCH_ENABLED=true, ./deploy-infra.sh (the namespace and its policies), ./apps/database/deploy.sh (the export's login and Secret db-svc-research-export), ./apps/research/deploy.sh, ./apps/backup/deploy.sh, ./apps/research-export/deploy.sh. Then a qa person reserves the held-out ranges before the first export, and the first export is started by hand or waits for 03:00 UTC (exercise E42). The rollback recipe sets it false and uninstalls the export, then the research database, keeping its volume.

The AI Workbench in the research zone (Phase 2b)

Status on 20 November 2026: deployed. The AI Workbench runs in the research zone since access policy version 8 (the skeleton version of research Phase 2b, approved by qa and applied on 20 November 2026), and its notebooks read the research snapshots through lake-api, with no identity and no path to the live database. Version 9, the change version, ended the scientists' live measurements and every Superset right the same day (Superset is stopped; its database is kept). Exercises E43 and E44 were run on 20 November 2026. Before that date the notebooks read the live database as described in Reading platform data from a notebook.

Phase 2b moves the AI Workbench (JupyterHub, its proxy and every notebook server) into the research namespace, so that a notebook works only on snapshots and cannot reach the operational services. Where the workbench runs is not a setting: it follows the applied access policy. The workbench is placed in the research zone as soon as the policy's network section has a research-zone pod for the hub; until then it stays in the platform namespace. The owner decided the details on 19 November 2026 (decision record).

WhatIn the platform namespace (until the switchover)In the research zone (after it)
Who may sign inUnchanged: the roles compiled from the access policy (admin, bio_scientist, control_scientist, engineer, qa), through the platform sign-in
What a notebook readsThe live database, as the person (device-code sign-in, client workbench-notebook)The snapshots of the research lake, through lake-api; no sign-in in the notebook, no credential anywhere in the workspace
Where a notebook may connectKeycloak and the configuration API, while both IAM database switches are onThe hub, lake-api, and the internet on TCP port 443 only (pip, GitHub, the VS Code download), never a private address, the Tailscale range or the link-local range
The hub administratorAdministers the hub and may also start a workspace of their ownAdministers the hub, gets no workspace: the hub refuses to start a server for an account whose only workbench right is administration ("Administration of the AI workbench gives no workspace: sign in with an account whose role uses the workbench.")
What the hub may do in the clusterThe chart's own rightsA Role of its own, medcea-hub: pods and volume claims (read, create, delete) and events (read); no Secrets and no Services (a Service it could create as a NodePort would open the snapshot reader to the LAN). The namespace's pod security baseline refuses any privileged pod it might create
PriorityPlatform prioritymedcea-research-low for the hub, its proxy and every notebook: evicted first when memory runs short
CertificateThe platform certificateworkbench-tls, issued by the platform's certificate authority for the workbench's address only
Client workbench-notebookEnabledDisabled, not deleted, once the policy no longer names it; a new install never creates it

The home folders move with the workbench: each person's claim-<name> is copied on the host into a new volume in the research namespace (Moving the AI workbench). The hub's own database starts fresh in the zone: hub users and the personal API tokens they made are gone, and each person is made again in the hub at their next sign-in. The administrator's own home (claim-admin) is not copied, because the administrator gets no workspace there; it stays on the host until removed by hand. The old homes in the platform namespace are kept, labelled as left behind by the move, until the administrator removes them.

Two things the scripts do when the policy and the cluster disagree:

  • The policy places the workbench in the zone, but it still runs in the platform namespace (between applying the skeleton version and the move): ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh changes nothing and says "the AI workbench moves with ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh --move"; ./deploy-infra.sh shows that line as "Still to do"; ./apps/iam/apply.sh records it as a deferred target (workbench) that --resume closes after the move. The reverse case (a later version moves it back) says "moves back with" the same command.
  • The policy places the workbench in the zone, but RESEARCH_ENABLED is not true: nothing is installed or changed ("skipped: the AI workbench lives in the research zone (the access policy) and RESEARCH_ENABLED is not true"), and a hub already running there is left running, unmanaged, with a warning.

The health check Workbench accounts lists hub users without an enabled platform account (offboarding is: deactivate the account, then remove the person from the hub, since their own hub API tokens outlive the account), and Research grants and Secrets checks that no pod of the research zone names a Secret outside its own short list and that no Role there grants Secrets (Health checks).

Reading snapshots from a notebook (Phase 2b)

The snapshot reader lake-api (./apps/lake-api/deploy.sh, run by ./apps/research/deploy.sh as its last step) is a small read-only web service in the research namespace in front of the research database. It answers only from read functions in the schema lake_api, which return the lake's rows and nothing else, and it holds no identity: by the owner's decision (O2 of 19 November 2026) the network decides who reaches it, notebooks and the host, and the database decides what it answers. Its database login, rs_lake_api, may only execute those functions, in read-only transactions of at most 30 seconds, with at most 10 connections. Nothing a person typed and no person is in the lake (The nightly export), so nothing personal can be read through it.

In a notebookReturns
md.connect()Pins the newest snapshot for the kernel and prints its provenance line (snapshot number, cut, contract version, lineage). In the platform namespace it signs in as before, so the same notebook runs in both places.
md.snapshots(), md.snapshot(n)Every snapshot, or one, with its cut, row counts, digests and lineage.
md.use_snapshot(n, expect=None)Pins snapshot n. With expect= a lineage, refuses the snapshot unless its lineage is that one (a result recorded with a lineage is recomputed on exactly the same data, even after the research database was rebuilt and its numbers started again).
md.measurements(unit, zone, tag="air_temperature", minutes=60, …)The readings of the pinned snapshot, newest first under the limit and returned oldest first, in the window that ends at the snapshot's cut, not now (a snapshot is up to a day old); start= and end= set the window instead. The columns are the platform mode's plus ingested_at and snapshot_id.
md.units(), md.zones(), md.recipes(), md.recipe_lines(), md.catalogue()The pinned snapshot's units, zones, approved and retired recipes with their lines and setpoints, and the quantity catalogue. Units and zones carry codes, not database ids or descriptions (a warning says so once).
md.holds()The held-out ranges: unit, zone, from, to. Never who made a reservation or why.
md.provenance(df)What a result came from (df.attrs["medcea"]): the snapshot, its cut and contract version, its lineage and whether the notebook recomputed it, the set's digest, the query, and a sha256 of the answer as received.

Lineage. Each snapshot's lineage is a sha256 chained over the measurements digests of every snapshot up to it (the first one's predecessor is empty), computed by the database from the append-only snapshot table, never stored. Two snapshots with the same lineage hold the same readings; a notebook recomputes it from md.snapshots() and says whether it agrees.

Runs, cycles, control loops and parameter sets are in the lake but not readable from a notebook. Phase 3 decided to keep them so (decision O3 of 20 November 2026): the calibration needs only measurements, recipes, recipe steps and the catalogue, and the lake holds no cycles and no control loops yet; exposing them is a change to lake_api.sql, not to the access policy, and is revisited with the step-test contract change or when Phase 4's agents need run history. md.sign_in() and md.sign_out() only print that the notebook no longer signs in. If lake-api does not answer, the helper says "the lake reader is not reachable (./apps/lake-api/deploy.sh)"; a refused query (an unknown snapshot, no unit or zone, a limit outside 1 to 50,000) gives the database's own message.

The health check Research lake reader checks the reader's database roles, that it answers from the host, and that the newest snapshot's digests can still be recomputed from its rows (lake.snapshot_digest_check).

Calibrating the sensor model from a snapshot (Phase 3)

The research plan said the chamber model's time constant, humidity and CO2 constants would be calibrated from the lake's measurements. The data does not allow it, and the owner decided on 20 November 2026 to build now and fit what is there: the whole pipeline is built (fetching a snapshot pinned by its lineage, fits that check what the data can identify, scenarios and manifests that name the snapshot), the sensor model is calibrated, and every plant constant stays an assumption that the fit refuses until step-test data exists (below). The reasons are in the data:

  • The lake's contract (version 1) exports the readings only: no state report from a CONTROL board and no command. The chamber has never had a CONTROL board, the lake holds no cycle and no control loop, and the room is not measured. A plant constant is seen only through what an actuator does to a reading against the room's conditions, so none can be fitted.
  • There is one unit and zone (UNIT01/ZONE01), about 14 hours (14 November 19:52 to 15 November 09:59 UTC), about 16,670 readings per sensor and quantity, from an SHT45 and an SCD30. There is no substrate sensor.
  • The board publishes about every 3 seconds, not every 30 as the model assumed; its silence after 15 November and the held-out range are outages, never lost messages.

Nothing here writes the lake or changes the platform: the commands read lake-api from the host and write only the files you name. There is no access policy change and no deploy.

Fetching a snapshot

apps/research/calibrate.sh snapshots
apps/research/calibrate.sh fetch --snapshot 1 --expect-lineage <64 hex> --unit UNIT01 --zone ZONE01 --out ~/calib/s1

calibrate.sh runs python3 -m research.calib (with research/.venv's Python when it exists). It logs to logs/research-calibrate-<time>.log and takes no lock. snapshots and fetch need RESEARCH_ENABLED true and a running lake-api, whose address it finds itself (exit 2 otherwise); every other subcommand runs without the cluster. ./medcea.sh offers the same under Applications → Calibrate the sensor model from a snapshot (list, fetch, fit), with a [Y/n] confirmation and no lock.

fetch refuses (exit 2, nothing written) unless the snapshot exists, its lineage recomputes from the snapshot list and equals the one you give, so a result recorded with a lineage is always fitted again on the same readings. It reads every reading of the unit and zone up to that snapshot in pages of 5,000 (--page-size; a 50,000-row page ran lake-api out of memory on 20 November 2026, and Kubernetes restarted it), and checks per snapshot: as many rows as the snapshot recorded means complete, and its measurement digest is recomputed (a mismatch refuses the fetch); fewer is marked incomplete, with the difference; more is refused. No row may lie inside a held-out range. It writes three files and never overwrites one:

FileContentCommitted
dataset.jsonlThe readings in a canonical order, with a header naming the snapshot, its lineage and digests, the query and the per-snapshot checks; no time of the fetch and no held-out range, so two fetches give the same bytes (its content_sha256).No (about 10 MB, refetched by its lineage)
extract.yamlThe snapshot's recipes, recipe steps and quantity catalogue, each value as the database wrote it, so python3 -m research.calib verify recomputes their digests offline.Yes, as research/calib/extracts/snapshot-<id>-<lineage 12>.yaml
fetch-log.jsonThe address, the time and the held-out ranges seen.No

Fitting the sensor model

python3 -m research.calib fit-sensors ~/calib/s1/dataset.jsonl --map sht45=sht45_1,scd30=scd30_1 \
    --name unit01-zone01-s1 --out ~/calib/unit01-zone01-s1.yaml --report ~/calib/report.txt
python3 -m research.calib fit-plant ~/calib/s1/dataset.jsonl
python3 -m research.calib verify ~/calib/unit01-zone01-s1.yaml

--map names which lake sensor each model sensor is. The fit takes the readings by board cycle (one timestamp per cycle, shared by every quantity of both sensors, stamped by the board) and splits them at outages (a gap of 60 seconds or more); a gap up to three cycles is normal, a longer one under 60 seconds a skipped cycle. The gaps are the board's own, read from its timestamps: the time the platform received a reading is used only for the latency, because the platform sometimes receives a run of cycles late and then all at once, which is a delivery stall, not a skipped cycle or an outage. Each value is fitted with a 95 % interval from a deterministic resampling, rounded to six significant digits, and applied only when the data supports it:

  • Publish interval: the mean of the normal gaps between the board's timestamps. The start offset is 0 for both sensors, which publish in the same cycle.
  • Latency: from the time the platform stored a reading minus the time the board measured it. It includes the board clock's offset from the host's, so it is recorded as fitted but confounded.
  • Noise: from how the second differences of a series grow with the lag, which separates the sensor's noise and the 0.01 rounding from the chamber's own slow variation. It is refused (the default stays, with the reason) when its interval includes zero, the fit is poor, or the first differences are positively correlated, which white noise on a slow process never gives: the SCD30's CO2 on snapshot 1 (correlation +0.172). The data still bounds a refused noise: white noise adds twice its variance to the first differences', so it is at most the square root of half their variance. When the model's default noise at the level the sensor read is above that bound, the data contradicts the default, and the bound is applied instead (source upper_bound, with no relative part), recorded under "not modelled" as noise that may be smaller still: the SCD30's CO2 on snapshot 1, 0.50 ppm against the datasheet's 25.6 ppm.
  • Lost messages: only a quantity missing from a cycle in which the same sensor published another; a value whose interval is wider than the value itself is weak and not applied.
  • Offsets: relative to the SHT45, the reference: it has the better datasheet accuracy, the SCD30 warms itself, and the loops use the SHT45 with the SCD30 as fallback. The SCD30 reads +2.04 °C and −7.03 %RH against it. Self-heating (the warmer sensor seeing the same water at a higher temperature) explains only about a third of how the humidity offset changes with humidity, so the model is a choice recorded in the file, humidity_model: constant_offset by default (two constant offsets), or --humidity-model self_heating (2.04 °C of self-heating plus a remaining humidity offset). Both models' predictions are recorded.
  • Absolute accuracy: no data says how far the SHT45 itself is from the truth. The file sets a per-run constant error from the datasheet (half the stated accuracy: 0.05 °C and 0.5 %RH for the SHT45, 25.6 ppm CO2 for the SCD30 at the level it read), drawn once per run from its own seeded stream.
  • Validity: the humidity range the SHT45 saw (51.35 to 55.33 %RH).
  • Not modelled, recorded for the reader: publish jitter, the delivery stalls, the skipped cycles, the chamber's fast variation, the sensors' resolution not being a clean 0.01, repeated values beyond what noise explains, and that the SCD30's absolute error is correlated with the SHT45's through the fitted offset.

The calibration file is canonical YAML: the source (dataset digest, snapshot, lineage), the code (commit, whether research/ was clean, the Python version and the blob hash of every file of the fit and the model), each value with its source (fitted, fitted_confounded, upper_bound, chosen, datasheet, not_identifiable), interval, and applied or the reason it was not, and one entry per plant constant with its current value and why it is refused. fit-sensors and fit-plant refuse while the code they run and record (research/calib/*.py, research/twin_plant/*.py) differs from the commit, unless --allow-dirty, which the file records; a calibration or extract written under research/calib/calibrations/ or research/calib/extracts/ is data and does not count, so the next fit runs without committing it first. verify checks a file offline: its form, every rule above, and whether its code still equals the checkout.

fit-plant lists every plant constant with what the dataset lacks and exits 3, writing nothing, while none is identifiable. On snapshot 1 every constant but the volume (a hardware fact) gets NO_ACTUATOR_DATA (the lake has no command or state report), NO_EXCITATION (no actuator step) and NO_AMBIENT (the room is not measured); the substrate's add NOT_OBSERVED, the fungi's respiration and water CONDITIONAL_REFUSED (they need a closed-chamber relaxation with the room and substrate measured), and the biological figures LITERATURE. The step-fit itself is built and tested on simulated step tests; a calibration file with a fitted plant value is refused in Phase 3 ("plant fits are applied from a later phase"), and one whose assumed value differs from the model's is refused too (change an assumption in the scenario, where it is visible).

Using a calibration in a scenario

A scenario takes the calibration and, optionally, a recipe step of a snapshot through two pins, whose paths are relative to the scenario file and whose files are checked by sha256:

calibration:
  path: ../../calib/calibrations/unit01-zone01-s1.yaml
  sha256: 791540a3…
  extrapolate:
    air_humidity: the snapshot's humidity was 51-55 %RH; the noise and the SHT45-SCD30 offset are assumed to hold at 80-95 %RH
recipe_line_from:
  extract: ../../calib/extracts/snapshot-1-096015bc225c.yaml
  sha256: 79be22b9…
  snapshot_id: 1
  lineage: 096015bc…
  recipe_id: 2
  seq: 3
  light: {light_on_minutes: 720, light_off_minutes: 720, why: the recipe file's 1/1 is a placeholder}

The campaign resolves both before it runs anything, and refuses (exit 2): a file whose sha256 differs; a value the calibration and the scenario both set; a humidity band, a starting humidity or a room humidity outside the calibration's range without extrapolate and its reason (the starting humidity is the scenario's initial value, else the room's, which the chamber starts from; an ambient disturbance that sets the room's humidity counts too); a calibration made from a dirty tree, unless --allow-dirty; recipe_line together with recipe_line_from; an extract whose catalogue differs from the repository's recipe_types.yaml; a snapshot or lineage that is not the extract's; a step whose photoperiod is a placeholder without light. Calibrated values are merged quantity by quantity over the model's defaults. The manifest's provenance repeats what each pin applied and why (What the manifest proves).

Two calibrated scenarios ship: smoke_air_temperature_calibrated and fungi_pleurotus_fruiting_calibrated. Snapshot 1 holds an approved Fungi recipe (recipe 2) whose step 3 has exactly the Pleurotus fruiting setpoints (air 10 to 21 °C, 80 to 85 %RH, CO2 500 to 1000 ppm, substrate 16 to 18 °C), so the fruiting scenario takes its setpoints from that step; its photoperiod in the recipe is the placeholder 1 minute on, 1 minute off, so the pin sets 12 hours each, with the reason. Both scenarios run at humidity above the fitted range and say so in extrapolate.

The step-test protocol

The plant constants can be fitted once a CONTROL board is fitted to the chamber and the step tests below have run. The protocol is designed, not run; the same text is in research/calib/STEPTEST.md.

Preconditions. The unit idle (no run waiting or running); the unit in test mode, proposed by an engineer and approved by qa as usual; the door closed; a dummy substrate, or none, for the first series; a room sensor, a second SENSE board outside the chamber in its own unit and zone (the slot's name is the owner's decision); NTP checked on both boards; and a step log with the time of every switch, written by hand until the export carries the actuators' events.

SeriesWhat is doneWhat it gives
1. Baseline2 hours, everything offThe drift and the noise with nothing running
2. HeaterOn for 5 hours (about two time constants), then off for 5 hoursThe time constant, the gain, the air node's heat capacity (with the heater's power measured by a plug meter) and the heat loss to the room
3. Air flow fanOn for 2 hoursThe air it exchanges (from the change in time constant and the CO2 decay), and its mixing once the substrate is measured
4. HumidifierOn for 30 minutesThe water it adds per hour
5. CO2 fanOn for 1 hour after CO2 has built upThe air it exchanges
6. Closed chamberCO2 and humidity left to relax with the room measuredThe leak; with substrate and a DS18B20, the fungi's CO2 production
7. Cooler, lamps, substrate heaterAs the heater, when fittedTheir powers and effects

Each series is repeated twice, with at least two time constants of rest between steps (about 2.4 hours each, so plan two days). A 2-hour heater step is not enough: with the chamber's own fast variation as measured in snapshot 1, the fit's time constant was off by up to about 10 % on simulated 2-hour steps, and the fit refuses about a third of them as too uncertain (its interval is widened for the chamber's own wander, so the steps it accepts are covered: about 96 % of them, against 67 % before the review of 20 November 2026), while the 5-hour step gave it within about 2 %.

The contract change it needs (a later phase, with its own skeleton version approved by qa): two new read functions on the platform side for the boards' state reports and the commands (when, which unit and zone, which actuator, which state or command, from a loop or test mode; no person), the export's contract version 2, a new lake table with its digest and a new lake-api function. fit-plant already takes that shape.

The comparisons on the calibrated model

The two comparisons were run again on the calibrated sensor model, with the same grids, seeds and clock offsets as their uncalibrated pairs, in research/.venv (FLC and MPC on their own libraries) at commit d692ebf (the calibration refitted after the review of 20 November 2026; the first run, at d45d141 with the earlier calibration, gave 9995399f… and 31c9cb8f…), on 20 November 2026:

SpecRunsResult digest
e39_compare.yaml (E39's own spec, uncalibrated)30, 0 invalida96b20d1…, the same as E39
e39_compare_calibrated.yaml30, 0 invalid3b9017a5…, the same at --jobs 1
fruiting_compare.yaml45, 0 invalid3bf1f956…
fruiting_compare_calibrated.yaml (--max-cpu-hours 14)45, 0 invalidcd60adc0…

Read these with care. The metrics are computed on the model's true values; calibration changes only what the controllers see (a reading every 3 seconds instead of 30; far less noise, 0.012 °C instead of 0.05 °C on the SHT45 and 0.50 ppm instead of about 25 ppm on the SCD30's CO2; the SCD30's offsets). The plant is the same assumed model in both halves, so a difference is a sensor effect, never evidence about the real chamber. No run used the SCD30 as fallback (the SHT45 never went stale), so its offsets did not reach a controller, and no FLC or MPC run fell back to on/off control.

Means per run, uncalibrated → calibrated (distance from the middle, rmsd_mid, in °C and %RH; time next to an edge, boundary_hugging; command changes summed over the loops; energy):

ControllerSmoke, 1 h: air temperatureSmoke: humiditySmoke: energyFruiting, 48 h: humidityFruiting: humidity next to an edgeFruiting: command changes
If-Then-Else1.60 → 1.64 (next to an edge 0.49 → 0.61)2.13 → 1.8328.3 → 27.5 Wh1.71 → 2.010.135 → 0.4952,500 → 7,320
PID0.287 → 0.1561.31 → 1.0685.7 → 59.2 Wh1.09 → 0.760.045 → 0.0041,540 → 2,680
Q-learning1.93 → 1.9320.8 → 20.764.1 → 64.5 Wh8.21 → 7.080.120 → 0.15017,000 → 20,100
FLC0.114 → 0.1280.804 → 0.77492.2 → 82.8 Wh1.55 → 0.900.144 → 0.0011,020 → 2,440
MPC0.112 → 0.1330.870 → 0.68283.2 → 62.8 Wh1.55 → 0.880.148 → 0.0004753 → 2,680
  • PID, FLC and MPC hold humidity closer to the middle of its band on the fruiting scenario, and PID and MPC use less energy on the smoke scenario (more OFF commands).
  • Every controller changes its command more often on the 48-hour run (1.2 to 3.6 times), not less as the design expected from smaller noise: with a reading every 3 seconds the controllers see small real changes sooner. If-Then-Else sits next to the humidity band's edge much more of the time.
  • The air temperature on the fruiting scenario stays about 4.6 °C from the middle for PID, FLC and MPC and 5.7 °C for If-Then-Else in both halves: the room is warm and the model's cooler has no headroom. Energy there is about unchanged (2,490 to 3,310 Wh).
  • PID's dependence on the clock's origin is unchanged (PID depends on the clock).

The folders are reproduced by the commands of exercise E45; a run on the host's own Python marks the 12 FLC and MPC runs of the smoke comparison invalid, as in E39 (calibrated result digest f6ba09a1…).

Measuring the local model (Phase 4, step 0)

Before anything is built around a local language model, its speed on this host and how well it calls tools are measured. The host's processors have AVX but not AVX2, so llama.cpp runs its slowest x86 variant (sandybridge), and every figure in the design is an estimate until this step has run. The owner's choice (21 November 2026) is Qwen3-8B, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the fallback, decided by these measurements. Nothing here is a deploy: the step runs in the platform namespace, outside the research zones, at low priority, and leaves nothing running.

./apps/research-model/bench.sh plan            # what bench measures, its runtime and the cap; runs nothing
./apps/research-model/bench.sh fetch           # the two pinned models, about 7.5 GB
./apps/research-model/bench.sh bench --models 8b   # llama-bench, up to 4 hours
./apps/research-model/bench.sh bench --models 4b   # the same for the fallback, up to 4 hours
./apps/research-model/bench.sh eval            # the offline tool-call eval, about 1 to 3 hours
./apps/research-model/bench.sh report          # research/agents/bench/<date>.json (bench and eval write it too)
./apps/research-model/bench.sh cleanup         # the Jobs and Pods it made; never the models

The same steps are in ./medcea.sh → Applications → Benchmark the local model, and as exercise E51.

StepWhat it does
fetchJob research-model-fetch (the pinned Python image) downloads each model from its pinned Hugging Face revision into the model folder (RESEARCH_MODEL_DIR, by default /var/lib/<project>/research-models, created mode 700 for the deploying account; never inside the volumes' folder). A broken download resumes. The file is named after its sha256 and renamed into place only once its hash is the pin's; a mismatch is removed.
benchJob research-llm-bench (the pinned llama.cpp image) first starts llama-server once to read its system_info line, which must show AVX = 1 | AVX2 = 0. Then llama-bench measures, per model and in this order: the prompt speed (512 and 4,096 tokens) and the generation speed (128 tokens) on an empty context, the 512/128 tests again with 4,096 and then 12,288 tokens already in the context (all at 6 threads, one per physical core, without a NUMA strategy), and last, as an optional sweep, 512/128 at 12 threads and with --numa isolate. The measurements the design needs therefore come first, and a bench that is stopped keeps them. The threads are pinned to one processor: one hardware thread per core for 6 threads, both hardware threads of each core for 12. Under --numa isolate llama.cpp moves its threads to all of the processor's hardware threads at every step, whatever the pin says, so those rows are marked "node affinity" in the report, not "pinned".
evalPer model, Pod research-llm-eval-<model> runs llama-server (greedy, one slot, the model's own chat template, thinking off) with a one-time key, and this host sends it 16 fixture conversations (research/agents/evals/fixtures/): the tools the planned simulation and lake servers will offer, a standing policy, and recorded tool results, among them requests over budget, a malformed result and prompt injections inside tool results. No lake data and no session are used. Each answer is graded on this host: tool calls that parse and match the declared schema, campaign specs the harness accepts, CPU-hour budgets respected, no call to a tool that was not offered, the injection not obeyed. A 5-turn conversation measures whether the server reuses the cached prompt from turn to turn. The Pod and the key are removed at the end.
reportWrites research/agents/bench/<date>.json from every bench and eval of that day: the machine's facts, the pins, every measured rate (each bench run kept under its own name, so a bench of one model never removes the other's), the eval scores, the prefix-reuse verdict, and the recommendation. The file is evidence to commit; the research sandbox's check for uncommitted changes leaves it out, so campaigns and calibration still run before it is committed.

What it measured (21 November 2026). With an empty conversation, Qwen3-8B generates about 2.0 tokens a second and reads about 9.7; Qwen3-4B about 3.8 and 18. Both slow down sharply as the conversation grows: at 4,096 tokens of context 0.63 and 0.74 tokens a second, at 12,288 tokens about 0.25 for either model, so a 150-token answer then takes about ten minutes. Model size stops mattering at that point: the cost is in reading the conversation cache, which these processors (without F16C) convert the slow way. So agent sessions keep their conversation short, about 4,000 tokens at most, and Qwen3-4B is the provisional model; the tool-call eval runs in 4b against the real model server (owner decision of 21 November 2026, decision record).

The recommendation. Nothing is recommended until both the bench and the eval are in (both models' evals, finished). Qwen3-4B is recommended when Qwen3-8B generates below 1.5 tokens a second or processes prompts below 3 tokens a second, or when Qwen3-8B is clearly worse (15 points or more below the 4B model) on any graded outcome of the eval: the share of conversations passed, valid tool calls, valid campaign specs, budgets respected, refusals respected, injections resisted. Otherwise Qwen3-8B. The prefix-reuse check counts a turn as reused only when the server did not process the model's own previous answer again. The owner decides; the report is the evidence.

Refusals. plan, bench and eval print the estimated runtime first and refuse (exit 2) when its pessimistic end is above --max-hours (4 hours by default). The estimate counts the attention over every query head and, since this host's processors lack F16C, twice the context-dependent cost (an assumption the bench replaces). One model's bench fits (about 2.3 hours expected and 3.9 pessimistic for Qwen3-8B); both together do not (about 3.7 and 6.4), so run --models 8b and then --models 4b, or measure less with --threads 6, --numa none or --depths 0,4096. A bench's Job stops by itself 30 minutes after the cap; the eval has one end time for all its models, and each model's Pod gets what is left of it. bench and eval refuse while a recipe run is running or scheduled (R or S), and read the runs again every 5 minutes while they run: a run that starts stops the bench's Job or the eval's Pod ("stopped: run N started"), and what was measured stays in the report. With --during-run (owner decision of 21 November 2026: a fruiting run lasts days) they go on beside a running or scheduled run instead: they list the runs, mark every measurement as taken during one (during_run in the report), and every 5 minutes check that the host keeps 3 GiB of memory available and a 1-minute load at most 2 below its processor count, else they stop the Job or the Pod the same way. They also refuse while the host has less memory available than the Job needs plus 2 GiB (10 GiB for the bench, 12 GiB for the 8B model's server). fetch, bench, eval and cleanup take the deploy lock; bench holds it until it ends, so no deploy runs during a measurement. Stopped with Ctrl-C (or closing the terminal), bench and fetch delete their Job and eval its Pod before they exit, so nothing runs on without the lock.

It shares the processors with production. The Jobs run under nice 19 with a small processor request and no limit, so every pod that requests processor time comes first. The scheduler, the ingress and several other production pods request none yet (owner decision OD24, not built), and those share the processors with the bench as equals; that is why it refuses while a run is active. Run it when the chamber is idle, or with --during-run, whose numbers are kept apart as taken beside a run.

How the agent will work (Phase 4, design)

Phase 4 adds a supervised agent: a scientist starts it from a notebook, it plans simulations and runs them within a CPU budget, reads lake snapshots, and ends with a proposal. Every step is recorded in a tamper-evident trace that can be replayed, and nothing it produces reaches production without qa. The figure is the design decided on 21 November 2026; only the notebooks, lake-api and the research database run today. Solid boxes are running, dashed grey boxes come in 4a (with a scripted agent, no language model), dashed amber ones in 4b (the local model) or later. The numbers follow the order of the work.

The work, in order.

  1. Start. In a notebook, the scientist runs medcea-agent start with a profile (for example "compare controllers") and a CPU budget.
  2. Sign in and get a session. The orchestrator relays a device sign-in to research-session, which checks the person and their scientist role with Keycloak and mints a session token: up to 8 hours, a fixed tool list and budget, at most two sessions per person.
  3. The agent starts. The orchestrator starts one agent Job. Only that pod can claim the token, which is bound to its address and revoked when the Job ends.
  4. Think. Each turn goes to the model through the gateway: the local Qwen3-8B in 4b, a scripted agent in 4a. Tool output is wrapped as untrusted data, so text inside a result is never taken as an instruction.
  5. Plan a campaign. The agent asks mcp-sim for an estimate. mcp-sim recomputes the CPU cost itself and applies the gate: below 2 CPU-hours it runs at once; above, the scientist approves it in the CLI; above 24 it is refused.
  6. Simulate. A simulation Job runs the chamber twin with production's own controllers, under a hard CPU-hour cap and deadline, and reports metrics and a result digest.
  7. Look at real data. Through mcp-lake the agent reads person-free lake snapshots with fixed queries, never the live platform.
  8. Everything is recorded. Every turn, tool call and result, gate decision and proposal is appended by research-session to the agent_trace hash chain. The nightly backup anchors its head, and a replay of the session must give the same results byte for byte.
  9. A proposal, never a change. The agent ends with a proposal (for example a tuned PID parameter set) that stays in the trace. From Phase 6 an engineer can import it as a draft, and only qa's approval lets a unit run it.

What keeps it safe.

  • Proposals only. The agent has no route to the scheduler, the boards, MQTT or the recipes. Its output is a record to review.
  • Budgets and a human gate. Turns, tokens, CPU-hours and wall time are capped per session (16 CPU-hours by default). Large campaigns wait for the scientist's approval, and the caps are enforced while simulations run, not only estimated.
  • Isolation. The agent machinery runs in its own namespace, which the notebook hub cannot create pods in. The signing key and the trace writer live in a third. The agent has no service account, no secret and no internet.
  • Tamper-evident and replayable. The trace is append-only and hash-chained, written only by research-session, with the writer chosen by network port, never by what the agent claims. Strict replay checks every recorded step.
  • Production comes first. Everything runs at the lowest priority, inside quotas, with the model on 6 cores of one processor. Governance (AI inventory, a risk assessment per profile, the oversight procedure) is recorded before the first session.

Names are the design's (codeplan/rs4-design.md, with its revisions after review) and may change while it is built. Before 4a is built, step 0 measures the local model on this host (Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B on llama.cpp, processors with AVX only).

Agent sessions (Phase 4a)

Built on branch research/phase-4 and not deployed. Everything that runs on the cluster waits for the skeleton version of the access policy (the two zones, their pods and hops, the group research_campaigns, the Keycloak client research-agent), which qa must approve first; until it is applied each new deploy script prints one skip line and changes nothing.

What is built.

  • Two namespaces. research-gw holds research-session: it mints and checks session tokens and is the only writer of the agent_trace hash chain. research-agents holds research-orchestrator (starts and stops sessions, creates the Jobs), mcp-sim and mcp-lake (the agent's only tools), the research-runs volume and the Jobs agent-* and sim-*. Neither can be reached from the notebook hub's namespace except through the compiled hops; the Jobs have no service account, no Secret and no internet.
  • The tools. sim.estimate, sim.run, sim.status, sim.results and lake.snapshots, lake.summary, lake.catalogue. sim.run is the gate: mcp-sim recomputes the estimate itself, runs a campaign below 2 CPU-hours at once, makes it wait for the supervisor above that, and refuses one above 24. The estimate of a PID, bang-bang or Q-learning spec is computed inside mcp-sim; an FLC or MPC spec needs their libraries, so mcp-sim asks the orchestrator for an estimate Job (estimate-<id>, 250m CPU, 1 GiB, ten minutes at most, no network): the same short calibration slice per scenario and controller, run in an image that has scikit-fuzzy and gekko. sim.estimate waits for it up to 300 seconds and then answers that the Job did not finish; if the libraries are missing the Job refuses rather than price a bang-bang fallback. The sim Jobs of an FLC or MPC campaign install the same libraries. They are hash-pinned wheels (apps/research-agents/requirements-controllers.txt, python 3.14, the same pins as the host venv) that ./apps/research-agents/deploy.sh downloads once, into the same wheel folders as the service wheels; only the sim and estimate Jobs install them, the service pods stay lean.
  • The trace. Every turn, tool call, result, gate decision and checkpoint is an event in agent_trace.event, hash-chained over all sessions, written only through one function whose allowed events depend on the network port the call arrived on. Strict replay of a finished session checks each recorded step.
  • The backup. The nightly backup records the chain's newest event, its hash and the database's identity in its MANIFEST (# agent_trace chain head) and also copies the research-runs volume (volumes/research-agents-research-runs.tar.gz).

The commands. From a notebook, medcea_agent.py (a byte-for-byte copy of research/agents/cli.py, delivered with the examples) is from medcea_agent import Client; from a terminal that has the repository it is python3 research/agents/cli.py:

medcea-agent signin                              # device code, through the orchestrator's relay
medcea-agent start compare_controllers           # prints the session id
medcea-agent watch SID                           # follow the trace until the agent stops
medcea-agent approve SID GID [--cap-h H]         # the gate: only the supervisor who started it
medcea-agent deny SID GID
medcea-agent stop SID                            # revokes the session, deletes its Jobs
medcea-agent replay SID                          # strict replay, run as a Job; waits for its verdict

Your tokens stay in the process's memory. The gate id GID is printed by watch when a campaign waits. Only the person who started a session may approve or deny at its gate, and approving sets the CPU-hour cap for that campaign (never more than 24).

The health checks. Five were added (76 in all; Local model makes 77, see The local model): Research gateway network policies and Research agent network policies (the two zones' policies equal the compile), Agent trace chain (verify_chain() and an independent recomputation), Agent trace anchor (the newest backup's head is still in the chain with the same hash; a backup of another database only warns) and Agent sessions (the services run, the key id is the Secret's, and the last event research-session wrote is in the database with the same hash; a mismatch is a FAIL). Research grants and Secrets also scans both new namespaces.

Replay. c.replay(sid) (or medcea-agent replay SID) asks the orchestrator to replay a stopped session of yours (a running one is refused). The orchestrator reads the session's events from research-session and starts Job replay-<id>, which has no network, no Secret and no volume but the code: the events travel in the Job's environment (compressed; a trace too large for that is refused with the advice to replay on the host), the profile, standing text and skill come from the code bundle it runs. The Job prints one verdict line, the orchestrator records it in the trace as replay_result and returns {ok, first_mismatch, events}; the call waits and asks again every few seconds until then. A session run under another commit than the deployed one reports that as its first mismatch (the recorded digests differ), it never passes.

Not yet live. The policy version (qa approval), the first deploy of ./apps/research-agents/deploy.sh, the local model (Phase 4b). Exercise E48 is written for the day they are.

The local model (Phase 4b, stages 1 and 2)

The agent can think with a language model that runs on this host's CPU, inside the platform: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Q4_K_M, Apache-2.0), served by llama.cpp (server-b12182, by digest). The owner chose the 4B model and a context of 4096 tokens after the measurements of step 0, so a local session is a short one. Stage 1 built the model's server, its switch and its health check; stage 2 added the gateway that connects an agent to it and the agent's local backend (below). The access policy version that admits both pods comes later: until the policy has the pods, nothing here installs.

What runs. ./apps/research-model/deploy.sh puts Deployment and Service research-llm in the research gateway namespace (RESEARCH_GW_NAMESPACE): one llama-server, one slot, greedy sampling, no API key and no internet. It asks for 6 CPUs (no CPU limit, low priority) and 6 GiB of memory; about 3.7 GB is in use at a 4096-token context. An init container checks the model file's sha256 against the pin and that the CPU has AVX at every start, so a wrong file never starts a server. The file (about 2.5 GB) lives on the host in RESEARCH_MODEL_DIR (default /var/lib/<project>/research-models, mode 700, yours) and reaches the pod as a read-only volume; the deploy downloads it through ./apps/research-model/bench.sh fetch when it is missing (resumable, checked against the pin).

The gateway and the local backend (stage 2). A session never talks to research-llm itself: it asks model-gateway (Deployment and Service in the same namespace, port 8120, installed by the same ./apps/research-model/deploy.sh after the model; its code is the ConfigMap model-gateway-code, and uninstalling removes it first). For each turn the agent sends the gateway the session token and the conversation so far. The gateway checks the token with the session service (a token only works from the pod it was given to), refuses a session whose prompt or output tokens are spent, translates the conversation into the model server's chat request, and answers with the model's text and at most one tool call. The request is always the same fixed greedy setting (temperature 0, top-k 1, seed 1, thinking off, prompt cache on); the answer length is whatever the session has left, at most 1,024 tokens. There is one slot: while one turn runs, another session is told busy (429) and the agent waits and asks again, the wait counting against its wall-clock cap. A call the model wrote badly (a tool that does not exist, arguments that are not an object, two calls, a call written as plain text) comes back as text flagged as an error; the agent treats it as a refused call and the model sees the refusal on its next turn. If the model's context is full the session stops with context_full.

What is recorded, and by whom. For a local session the agent does not write the model's two records; the gateway does, under its own name (model-gateway): turn_request (the request's digest, the model pin and the fixed settings) before the call and turn_response (the response, its digest, the raw answer's digest and the model server's own token counts) after it. If the trace refuses a record, the turn is refused and nothing is returned that the trace does not hold. A failed model call is recorded as an error response. Everything else (tool calls, results, checkpoints, the stop) is the agent's, as in a scripted session. The profile compare_controllers_local asks for the same tools and the same CPU-hour cap as the scripted one, with 8 turns, 2 hours of wall-clock and 4,000 tokens of context (a local profile may not ask for more than 4,096); the task is the first message of the conversation. The orchestrator refuses to start a local profile (409) while no gateway is configured, that is while RESEARCH_LOCAL_MODEL is not true when ./apps/research-agents/deploy.sh runs.

Replay. A local session is replayed from the gateway's recorded responses instead of the agent's, and each rebuilt request must have the digest the gateway recorded. That proves the agent loop, the tool results and the caps behaved as recorded. It does not prove that the model would answer the same again: running the model a second time is a separate measurement, never the evidence.

The switch. RESEARCH_LOCAL_MODEL (false by default; an older config.env without the line reads false). Switch it with ./medcea.sh → Applications → Turn the local model on or off: enable sets it true, runs ./apps/research-model/deploy.sh and ./health-check.sh; rollback sets it false and runs ./apps/research-model/uninstall.sh, which removes the server and keeps the model file. The deploy prints one line and exits 0 (nothing installed) while RESEARCH_ENABLED or RESEARCH_LOCAL_MODEL is not true, the applied access policy has no research-llm pod, no policy version is applied, or the namespace is missing. It refuses unless the zone's compiled network policies are live.

The health check. Local model only reads: it never asks the model to generate. SKIP while the switch is false. FAIL when the Deployment's or the server's model is not the pin in apps/research-model/pins.json. WARN when the pod is not Ready, /health or /props do not answer, the context is not 4096 or the server reports no chat template, when RESEARCH_LOCAL_MODEL is true but there is no Deployment, or when generation since the start is below half the bench's measured rate.

The access policy version (stage 4). The local model's two pods need network rules before they can run under the applied policy: model-gateway (port 8120, reached by the agent job and by this host's health probe; it reaches research-llm on 8080 and research-session on its server port 8102) and research-llm (port 8080, reached by the gateway and by this host; it reaches nothing). The agent job gains one hop, to the gateway, and the gateway one public route, POST /v1/turn, protected by the session token. This is a skeleton-only version: no group, no cell, no Keycloak client, and no person role gains anything, so any qa person may approve it. It is proposed and approved by nobody yet; until it is applied the two pods stay denied by the zone's default rule and the local backend cannot start. The decision is in the decision record.

Not built yet

PhaseWhat it adds
2bDeployed 20 November 2026, versions 8 and 9 (above): the skeleton version that places the AI Workbench, its notebooks and lake-api in the research zone and removes the notebooks' live path, then the move, then the change version that ends the scientists' live data and every Superset right (the live Superset stops). The orchestrator first planned here moved to Phase 4 (owner decision O1 of 19 November 2026): until then scientists run campaigns in their own notebook.
3Built 20 November 2026 (branch research/phase-3, not deployed: nothing on the cluster changes; owner decision "build now, fit what's there"): the sensor model calibrated from snapshot 1, scenarios pinned to a calibration and a snapshot's recipe step, manifests that name them, and the comparisons run again (above). Still to come: the plant constants, once a CONTROL board is fitted and the step test has run (The step-test protocol), which needs the export to carry actuator events (a later skeleton version).
4The orchestrator that runs simulations as Kubernetes Jobs, and the agent harness with the local model: a supervised agent runs a campaign through the orchestrator. The research services that check the route table themselves come with it. Step 0, the measurement of the local model, is built (branch research/phase-4, not run yet: above).
5The hosted model, through a gateway with recorded egress.
6The candidate registry and the promotion gateway: a tuned parameter set reaches the platform as a draft with its evidence on the policy history, for qa to approve. No MPC or FLC candidate is promoted while the scheduler lacks their libraries.
7The validation vault, which only the validation job reads.
