It is refused when K's rows under today's skeleton give any role more than under the skeleton K was approved under (OA-c); rows naming a retired group or role are dropped and counted. Pending account decisions are listed, not refused. Evidence: exercise E19, 5 November 2026 (training chapter, "Last done"): version 14 restored version 12 (event 215) and was confirmed by svieira, who did not run it (event 216); the health check warned until then.OA-c: a rollback restores what was approved, never more; confirmed after the fact because the point of a rollback is speed.
A failed rollout is reverted, a skeleton version is not (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)After three failed attempts a change or rollback version is reverted in a second transaction, which files the unfinished revert under the previous version first, so an interruption at any point is resumable (--resume converges forward, never reverts). What a revert does not undo: retired MQTT person credentials, pgAdmin sessions ended by a claims change, narrowings access-api applied in the window (health WARNs until qa reviews them). A skeleton version's failed rollout is left partial_apply {mixed}: the accepted skeleton moved and HEAD carries it; undoing it is a git revert plus a deploy, which accepts it as a narrowing.Owner decision 3 of 4 November 2026.
The health baseline of an apply (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)Before the question, apply.sh runs the artefact checks it runs after the apply (eight; nine from Superset stage C, which adds Superset roles). For apply.sh N any FAIL refuses ("fix them first"); for a rollback it is reported and never drives a revert. After the apply only a check that was not FAIL before counts.Owner decision 13: a check failing for reasons no policy version causes must not revert a correct apply.
Dual control read from the policy (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The User Manager takes who approves and who makes account and policy changes from the route table's dual_control, compiled from the policy, instead of its own list; without the key it keeps qa and admin.One source of the rule (S-E1).
The history's head outside the database (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The policy history's head (event id and hash) is written into the apply log, into every applied event (chain_head_before) and into each nightly backup's MANIFEST. Residual: a superuser who disables the triggers and re-hashes the chain from an edited event onward is found only by comparing with those copies (§16 of the design), not by verify_chain().S-F1: anchor the head where the database's superuser cannot rewrite it.
Role composites at apply (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)apply.sh compares Keycloak's composite roles with the accepted skeleton's includes ("Keycloak's role R includes …, the accepted skeleton …: ./deploy-infra.sh adds the composites") and refuses a skeleton version that changes includes ("not applied in 4.5"): ./deploy-infra.sh only adds composites, so nothing could apply the change.Owner decision 4 of 4 November 2026: compiling the composites from the policy is left to a later slice.
A rotated realm key, and someone left to approve (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)An approval whose signing key Keycloak no longer publishes is refused with "withdraw version N and draft again" (an approved version cannot be returned). After the version, an enabled account must still hold an approver role of iam_policy and of iam_users whose person is not an enabled maker's: a refusal for apply.sh N, a warning for --rollback-to, which must not be blocked and is confirmed afterwards.Owner decisions 6 and 7 of 4 November 2026.
Reuse of an approval token (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)A token id (jti) is refused only when another version's approved evidence holds it. Accepted residual: a captured confirm or dispute token could be replayed at an approve within its 300-second life.Owner decision 12 of 4 November 2026: the strict rule would refuse an honest approve made after a confirm in the same session.
How the approval check is tested (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The signature and Keycloak checks are tested offline (fixed RS256 vectors, a fake Keycloak) and live (tests/iam-policy.sh --apply, exercise E19); the throwaway database fixture runs the bundle with unsigned evidence. Production code has no second, test-only key path. The live runs found what the offline tests could not: PostgREST stores the claims with the role it took (anon), so the exact comparison refused every real approval at apply (found by tests/iam-policy.sh --change, fixed in d1a4c48) and failed the audit of a real approval (found by E19, fixed the same day); both now decide by one rule, source.claims_recorded, which accepts that one added key and nothing else.Owner decision 8 of 4 November 2026.
A deploy after an unfinished rollout (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)./apps/iam/deploy.sh resumes an apply left at apply_started by itself, but only warns on partial_apply ("ended in partial_apply: ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you>"): a mixed or reverting outcome wants a person to look first.Owner decision 9 of 4 November 2026.
The backup's chain head, read before the dump (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)The nightly job reads the policy history's head before pg_dump, so the dump holds at least that event; a restore whose chain ends below it, or carries another hash there, was cut or rewritten after the backup (backups.sh restore-help prints the comparison). An exact snapshot (pg_dump --snapshot) would need a held connection in the job's shell.Owner decision 10 of 4 November 2026.
What exercise E19 changes on this install (IAM 4.5, 5 November 2026)E19 narrows one cell of a role no account on this install holds (maintenance or qc), chosen with the live test's guard (only routes and grants change), and rolls it back. Its effect is shown by the applied event's changed list, the moved route-table digest and the role's lost privilege, not by a person's refusal. As in E16 to E18, its accounts belong to one human, so it proves the mechanism, not independent review. Done 5 November 2026 with maintenance R on device_history (versions 13 and 14).Owner decision 11 of 4 November 2026: the full mechanism, no effect on anyone's access.
The Node-RED editor's Logout signs out of the platform (5 November 2026)The editor's Logout continues, after the editor has ended its own session, through the same chain as the user menu's Sign out: Node-RED's sign-in gate, the platform sign-in's "Do you want to log out?" page (client node-red), then the AI Workbench's logout when the workbench is installed, landing on the platform sign-in page. The address is fixed at deploy (NR_LOGOUT_URL), holds no sign-in token, and the editor takes only an https address. Decided by the platform owner on 5 November 2026, when the gap was found.Found live during exercise E15: after Logout, opening Node-RED again showed the engineer's flows at once. Logout ended only the editor's session; the sign-in gate's cookie and the platform sign-in stayed, and the editor's automatic sign-in took the same person straight back in. The next person on that browser could have acted, and deployed, under the engineer's name. The workbench had the same gap until 1 November 2026. Exercise E21 checks it.
Boards reach the broker over TLS only (5 November 2026)Boards connect to the broker on port 31884, TLS only. Each board checks the broker's certificate against the platform's certificate authority, copied to it at onboarding, and by the name mqtt.<domain>, before it sends its password. The certificate is issued by ./deploy-infra.sh from the same authority as the web certificate. The plain port 31883 was closed at once, not after a transition. Each message is not signed in addition: a publish is trusted because the board signed in over TLS with its own password and stays within its own slot's topics. Decided by the platform owner on 5 November 2026.Each board already had its own password and topic limits, but the password crossed the network in clear at every connection, so anyone on the network could capture it and publish as the board. No board was registered on the platform at the time, so closing the plain port at once cut nobody off. Signing every message would also guard against something inside the platform publishing forged readings, at the cost of key handling on the board, in Node-RED and in onboarding; the owner judged sign-in over TLS enough. Tried on an ESP32-S3 before it was built: the right certificate connects; a wrong name, a wrong authority, an expired certificate and a board clock at 2000 are refused. The health check's Mosquitto MQTT (TLS) watches it. Exercise E22 checks it; on 6 November 2026 in part: plain port closed, certificate verified by name, a board registered with the TLS settings; its own connection waits for its sensor (the board restarts before connecting while no sensor answers).
Onboarding checks the WiFi passphrase at once (5 November 2026)Right after the passphrase, the freshly flashed board joins the network itself; the run goes on only when it got an address, or when the person chooses to continue anyway. The passphrase field has a Show button. Files are copied with boot.py last and each copy is retried. Asked for by the platform owner on 5 November 2026.An onboarding ended with "wrong passphrase" after every file had been written. The passphrase was right: every copy restarts the board, which ran the boot.py already copied and started a WiFi sign-in that the next copy cut off, and after a dozen cut-off sign-ins the access point refused the board for minutes. The copy tool's errors were also discarded, and the last check ended on an error before the run's summary. All are fixed (training chapter, E22).
Back and Cancel in onboarding (5 November 2026)Back only on the questions before the board is touched (role, slot, wiring) and on the WiFi network and passphrase; Cancel at every step until the board's files are written, for the person who started the run only, never inside a flash write; after that the run always goes on to register the board and write its record, so the passwords just put on the board are kept. The platform's database is written only at the end of a run, so Back and Cancel leave no record behind; a cancelled run says what state the board was left in. Asked for by the platform owner on 5 November 2026, who chose Back before the erase only.A wrong answer in the planning questions meant abandoning the run in the browser, which left the script waiting. Back after the erase would re-ask questions whose effect on the board cannot be undone, so it is not offered there. Exercise E23 checks it; done on 6 November 2026 as expected. It also found that the wizard page's sign out left the portal's own session open for up to 4 minutes; since that day it follows the platform's one-hop sign-out (Keycloak, the AI Workbench, the portal), as the user menu does; checked live the same day.
Configuration records are retired, never deleted (5 November 2026)The Configuration UI has no Delete for locations, units, zones, devices or components; each form says to set Status to Inactive. Onboarding a slot again retires the earlier board's components instead of deleting them. Asked for by the platform owner on 5 November 2026.The access policy gives no person a DELETE grant on platform data (level D: records are retired), so under IAM_DB_ROLES=true every such Delete was refused, and a re-onboarding failed at its registration ("permission denied for table component", found that day). A retired record keeps the history, including the board's slot history.
Health and test messages are stored (6 November 2026)A SENSE board's health message (…/sense/_health) is stored in medcea.measurement with type HB, and a new test message (tag _test) with type TS. Both carry a reading's fields plus the board's IP and MAC address. Every board sends one test message at start-up; the host sends one as the board on request (the wizard's Send test message, flash-device.sh --send-test). The ingest flow takes the type from the topic, never from the message: only exactly sense/_health is HB and only sense/_test or control_setpoint/_test is TS; a message elsewhere that names either type is dropped with a warning in Node-RED's log. Migration 009 replaces the type's database check with the exact list AP, CT, SP, HB, TS. A sensor that fails no longer restarts the board: the health message says which one and why. Decided by the platform owner on 6 November 2026 (stored, the two types, the three senders); the topic rule's exact form and the drop by the implementer in the review the same day.The health message was built with the wiring screen, but the database's check refused it, so a sensor that failed showed nowhere but on the board's console; before that, a board with no working sensor restarted every 15 seconds and never connected (exercise E22). A test message proves a board's whole path (credential, topic rights, TLS, ingest) without waiting for a reading, and must be findable in the broker and in the database. Taking the type from the topic means no message, whatever it says about itself, can be counted as a reading or as a test that it is not. The old check was three pattern matches (a value containing AP, CT or SP, held to those three only by the column's two characters), not a list; rows outside the new list would leave the new check unvalidated (new rows still checked) with a warning rather than fail the deploy. The readers (Run Monitor, Grafana dashboards, the measurement views) select readings, commands and reports by type, so they show neither new type. Exercises E25 and E26 check it.
Hubs on one bus: the board closes the other hub's channel (review, 6 November 2026)The wiring check allows the same sensor address behind two different hubs on one bus (and behind two channels of one hub). The board makes that safe: before a hub opens a channel, every other hub on the bus closes its own; if one does not answer, the read is refused, naming that hub's address, rather than two sensors answering at once.Found in the review of the wiring screen: the check already allowed it, which is why a second hub is used, but the board left the other hub's channel open, so two sensors at one address could answer together. Fixing it on the board keeps the wiring the screen allows; refusing it in the check would have refused the reason for a second hub.
The SEN0562 light sensor's mode is written before every read (6 November 2026)The board writes the sensor's continuous high-resolution mode (0x10, the command of DFRobot's own example) before every reading, waits 180 ms and reads two bytes; lux is the raw value divided by 1.2.Found in the review: the sensor (a BH1750 inside) comes back from a power loss switched off and still answers with its last value, so a mode written once would publish a frozen reading with nothing to say it is wrong. The plan had named the one-time mode (0x20); the implementer kept DFRobot's command, written each time, which also starts a fresh measurement at every read. Whether it runs at 3.3 V is a bench check (exercise E25).
The bench-tested hub wiring is the shipped starting point (7 November 2026)The owner's I2C hub bench test (i2c_hub_test.py rev3, 6 November 2026, on the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1) passed with: hardware I2C(0) on GPIO 8 / 9 at 100 kHz with a 250 ms timeout, a TCA9548A at 0x70 (SparkFun Qwiic Mux BOB-16784) alone on the root bus, the SHT45 on channel 7, the SCD30 on channel 6, channels 0 to 5 empty. The platform ships that wiring as the board template Sense board as bench-tested 6 Nov 2026. The board firmware takes the test's timings on hardware I2C: a 250 ms bus timeout, an SHT45 soft reset at start and a read retried while the sensor is still converting, 4 ms between an SCD30 command and its read (the library's 1 ms is too short), and the SCD30's measurement interval set to 2 s before it starts, written only when the sensor holds another value (it is kept in the sensor's flash). For the owner to confirm (the implementer's choices, not part of the request): the wiring check no longer warns against the SCD30 on hardware I2C; software I2C gets the same 250 ms timeout, which is set but was never bench-tested (the test ran hardware I2C only); and the design map (SHT45 ch0, SCD30 ch1, SEN0562 ch2) stays as a second template, now on hardware I2C.The platform owner asked on 7 November 2026 for "a template that works", on the evidence of the bench test; the shipped bench template is that decision. The rest of this row is the implementer's reading of the test, listed for the owner to confirm. Software I2C with the SCD30, the SEN0562 and the chamber design map are not bench-tested yet; E25 records the first onboarding with the bench template.
Engineers' test messages from the MQTT Explorer (6 November 2026)Planned, not built. An engineer may send a test message to a board's sense/_test topic from the MQTT Explorer only after an approved skeleton version of the access policy adds it (proposed with apply.sh --propose-skeleton, approved by qa in the Access Policy, applied with apply.sh N), under the same condition as commands: only for a unit flagged for commissioning. Until then tests are sent from the wizard and the host only.The platform owner asked for this third sender on 6 November 2026. A person may today write only a commissioning unit's control topics; a sense topic gives a role more access, which the skeleton gate refuses on every deploy, so it can come only as an approved version (IAM 4.5).
A fixed LAN address for the platform host (14 November 2026)The host has the static address 192.168.1.200, set in netplan, instead of an address the router hands out. After the change the kubelet's certificate was renewed for the new address, ./deploy-infra.sh rewrote the network policies and the broker's certificate, and the health check passed all 65 checks. unit01-s-zone01 was onboarded again and connects to the new address; unit02-s-zone01 and unit02-c-zone01 were left as they are, by decision, and cannot reach the broker until they are onboarded again. Decided by the platform owner on 14 November 2026.A power cut on 14 November 2026 restarted the host, and the router gave it 192.168.1.208 instead of 192.168.1.207, which another device then held. The kubelet's certificate, the network policies and every board's broker address carried .207, so the cluster could not reach into its pods and no board could publish until each was fixed. With a fixed address a restart changes none of them. Known gap: the address must stay outside the router's DHCP pool, or the router may give it to another device (After a power cut the server has a new address).
AppArmor rules for containers on newer Ubuntu kernels (8 November 2026)The installer adds rules to MicroK8s's container profile instead of loosening the host: ./deploy-infra.sh installs a root-owned script and two systemd units that rebuild /etc/apparmor.d/cri-containerd.apparmor.d from MicroK8s's own profile plus four rules (signal and ptrace between processes of a container, with the plain and the stacked label, as the fix proposed upstream in containerd issue 14485), whenever MicroK8s rewrites it, and turn off Ubuntu's host profile mosquitto while the host has no Mosquitto of its own. kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined stays 1 and no pod runs unconfined. A health check (Container AppArmor, the first) fails while the rules are missing or a signal is refused inside a container. The host stays on kernel 7.0.0-38 until exercise E29 passes on the newer kernel. Decided by the platform owner on 8 November 2026. Installed on 9 November 2026 (E29 steps 1–4 on 7.0.0-38: units active, the rules put back within 4 seconds after a containerd restart, a second deploy changes nothing, all 57 health checks OK). E29 passed on the newer kernel the same day (steps 5–7): on 7.0.0-43 PostgreSQL ran under the stacked label the rules cover, 0 signals refused, Container AppArmor OK with no health failure; 7.0.0-43 is now the default kernel and the hold on 7.0.0-38 is lifted.Kernels 7.0.0-42 and 7.0.0-43 took the whole platform down on 8 November 2026: PostgreSQL hung in crash recovery, nginx could not reload, Mosquitto could not read its configuration. Setting the sysctl to 0 would turn off a hardening default for every program on the host, and running pods unconfined would drop their AppArmor confinement entirely; both were rejected. Writing the profile once would not last, because MicroK8s's containerd wrapper copies its own profile over it at every start, and containerd keeps a profile of that name once one is loaded, so the units put the rules back after each copy. The host profile mosquitto confines nothing on this host, which runs no Mosquitto of its own; if one is installed, it stays on and the health check names the container it attaches to. Known gap: until containerd ships its fix, each MicroK8s refresh relies on the profile still ending with its closing brace; the script refuses to change a profile of another shape, and the check fails.
Dialog boxes for ./guide.sh, the name ./medcea.sh, the end-of-command box and the MedCEA logo (9 November 2026)At a terminal the menus' questions are whiptail dialog boxes, each menu headed by a read-only status header (host, kernel, git commit, the last health check, the applied policy version, the deploy lock, the dry-run banner); the commands still run on the plain terminal. --plain, MEDCEA_PLAIN=1 (GUIDE_PLAIN=1 still accepted) and piped input keep the numbered mode unchanged. Then, the same day: the rename: ./guide.sh became ./medcea.sh, named after the platform, MedCEA, and not after PROJECT_NAME (an install with another project name runs ./medcea.sh too); ./guide.sh is kept for now as a forwarding alias that says so on stderr and runs ./medcea.sh with the same options and exit code, to be removed in a later release; every instruction, message and hint names ./medcea.sh, and the config.env.guide-<timestamp>.bak backups keep their name. The end-of-command box: with util-linux script installed, a command runs under script (its own terminal, so colours, sudo and its own questions work as before) and, when it ends, a box titled "Finished: exit code 0" or "Failed: exit code N" shows the command, the log it wrote and the last lines of its output, with Menu and Quit; a switch recipe or Bring IAM to full enforcement shows one box at its end, for all its steps; without script, the Enter prompt as before. The MedCEA logo: deploy-infra's banner moved into infra/lib-banner.sh; a compact version heads the first menu on a large terminal (never a sub-menu, left out when there is no room), the numbered mode prints the full one once at a terminal.Owner's choice: easier to read and harder to mis-type than numbered lists, with the platform's state in view before each choice. The questions, the checks on answers, the confirmations (a change defaults to No, a destructive command still wants yes typed) and what runs and is logged are the same in both modes; the header only reads files on the host, so it can neither change nor hold anything. Cancel or Esc in a question leaves the action with nothing run, and a box that fails ends the menus (exit 1): neither is ever taken as an answer (review of 9 November 2026). The name (owner's decision): the tool belongs to the platform, so its name must not change with an installation's project name; the alias spares existing notes and habits for one transition. The end box (owner's decision): the result and the output's end stay readable after the box clears the screen. What script records can include anything the command printed on the terminal, so the file is private (mode 600 in a mode-700 folder), read into memory and deleted as soon as the box is built, never kept, copied or logged; output holding the credentials box gets no box at all (the credentials stay on the terminal, and their text never reaches the box's command line, which other local accounts could read). The commands keep the deploy lock and its environment exactly as before (a recipe's steps still run under its one lock). Under script, Ctrl+C reaches only the command; a recipe step stopped so still stops the recipe (exit 130). The logo's tagline is now cyan, as always intended (the old check looked for "Medical"). Exercise E30.
Health checks of Phase 5: proving the applied policy is the one in force (9 November 2026)Scope of this round: four new checks, iamloaded (every running pod of the six route-checking services loaded the ConfigMap's route table), jwks (the Secret medcea-jwks holds exactly the realm's signing keys; always on; the key-id comparison moved here from postgrest, so a stale key fails once, not twice), kcscopes (the groups and medcea-identity scopes, their mappers, and both as default scopes on every platform client, read from Keycloak's database read-only; one client list, infra/lib-keycloak-clients.sh, for ./deploy-infra.sh and the check) and iamnetpol (the labelled NetworkPolicies by name against the compile), so 61 checks; and changes to existing ones: iamgrants no longer reads a drift as SKIP and, under IAM_DB_ROLES=false, warns of an unclassified table; iammqtt asks every iam-api pod; iampolicy warns when the Policy UI runs another compiler; noderedflows warns of flow files not committed to git; iamenforce fails without an enforce key and compares the switches recorded in settings.json with config.env (the file itself is not changed, so no service re-renders); iamchain warns when verify_chain() is not SECURITY DEFINER or not executable by iam_svc. FAIL only for what lets someone in, breaks token verification or proves a pod runs an outdated route table: a missing groups scope, groups mapper, audience mapper or person_id mapper on a client whose tokens reach a platform API (the User Manager's host clients, the token clients such as workbench-notebook, the onboarding wizard; mqtt-explorer counts, being a host client whose tokens reach iam-api); a realm RS256 key id the Secret lacks, or a Secret key id the realm no longer publishes; jwks-sig.json other than the signing keys of jwks.json; a service pod whose loaded route digest differs from the ConfigMap's for 120 seconds or more, or has none where the service enforces. Everything else WARNs: the same scope problems on a tool-only client (Grafana, pgAdmin, Superset, Node-RED, the workbench), an optional-only scope, full_scope_allowed off, uncommitted flow files, switches in settings.json other than config.env, an unclassified table under IAM_DB_ROLES=false, verify_chain() not SECURITY DEFINER or not executable by iam_svc, another compiler, IAM_NETPOL false (with or without labelled policies left), and a check that cannot read its source (a missing Secret medcea-jwks still FAILs). A realm that does not answer is a WARN in jwks, worded as the realm's problem (the Keycloak checks already FAIL it). The 120 seconds are counted from the ConfigMap's newest managedFields time (a time that cannot be read counts as past the 120 seconds). A pod with the current route digest and an older applied version is OK: the version is information only. Not this round: account drift between Keycloak and the database, an anchor for the chain head, a catalogue of the checks, a test of the documentation (account drift and the anchor came in the second round the same day, with a check of the database catalog: next row). Decided by the platform owner on 9 November 2026. Run on the live platform on 9 November 2026 (exercise E31, commit ed2b13f): all 61 checks OK, the four new ones with the expected texts; an uncommitted flow file WARNed in Node-RED flows vs git and cleared after git checkout.The health check said a policy version was applied, but nothing proved that the pods run its route table, that the keys and claims every token needs are in place, or that IAM_NETPOL is in force; and iamgrants could read real drift as SKIP. Failing on everything that is not final would turn every fresh install red; a FAIL is kept for what admits someone or refuses everyone, so it is acted on at once. Reading Keycloak's database instead of its admin API needs no token, writes no sign-in event and opens no port. Reading each pod with one kubectl exec that prints only a digest needs no change to the services. The four new checks prove the controls are in place, not that they work: tests/iam-hosts.sh, tests/iam-signin.sh and tests/iam-network.sh still test that.
Health checks of Phase 5, round 2: account drift, chain anchor, catalog (9 November 2026)Three new checks, so 64. Severity: the rule of the first round, extended: FAIL also for what proves tampering with, or drift of, the access records; everything else WARNs, and a check that cannot read its source WARNs. iamdrift (Account drift): the User Manager's service (access-api) computes the drift between Keycloak and the account record in the background, every 10 minutes (DRIFT_INTERVAL_SECONDS, never below 60; after a failed run it tries again after 2 minutes), with its existing service account and the one comparison the Decisions tab's banner already used (not a copy of it), in a read-only database session it rolls back and with no Keycloak write. It publishes only counts (accounts, unexplained roles, enabled while pending, failed compensations, unrecorded accounts), when it computed, whether the account list was cut, whether the seeded accounts could be read, and the kind of the last error: never a name, username, sub or e-mail. Keycloak's lists are read in pages up to a ceiling of 10000 accounts (before, 2000 at most, silently); reaching it is reported. New kind unrecorded account: an enabled account that no access request, account decision or status change names; service accounts never count. Exempt are seeded accounts only: those with an account_seeded fact (created, person_id_set or observed) on the policy history, matched by sub, by username only for a fact without a sub (./deploy-infra.sh records none without one). Nothing else is exempt: the test accounts of the 1 November install show until they are reviewed, as expected; the platform admin ADMIN_USER counts as seeded: the owner named it among the seeded accounts, and since 10 November 2026 ./deploy-infra.sh records it like the first qa person and the first engineer (a created fact when it creates it, else the one-time observed fact), so this round needs ./deploy-infra.sh once before ./apps/access/deploy.sh. (Built at first with an extra exemption, an account the latest signed-off access review listed; removed in review the same day, since the owner exempted seeded accounts only and the exemption lapsed at the next sign-off anyway.) A seeded account's role is explained by its seed fact: the role of its created fact, or for an account with none, its first observed fact (the one-time record of QA_USER, ENGINEER_USER and ADMIN_USER as they were); a later observed fact, which ./deploy-infra.sh records when it sees the role changed, explains nothing, so a role added in Keycloak outside the record is not laundered by the next deploy. Without this, a fresh install's seeded qa and engineer accounts would FAIL Account drift. A later decision replaces the seeded role as any later record does. The check reads the counts with one bounded, read-only kubectl exec into the access pod: FAIL on an unexplained role or a failed compensation; WARN on an account enabled while pending, an unrecorded account, a result older than 30 minutes, an error, a cut list, a fresh pod, and an access-api that predates the report, until ./apps/access/deploy.sh. iamanchor (History chain anchor): the chain head the newest complete nightly backup recorded in its MANIFEST (read before the dump since IAM 4.5) must still be in iam_policy.history with the same hash, read in one read-only session; FAIL when the event is missing or its hash differs; WARN when there is no backup or MANIFEST, the head cannot be read, the newest backup is older than 48 hours, or the backup folder is unreadable (it is mode 700: the check runs as the account that deployed the backup, never with sudo). After a restore from an older backup it FAILs until the next nightly backup. When the newest backup completed before the history's first event was written (a backup of an earlier database: BACKUP_DIR is kept across a new install and --purge-data), it WARNs that there is no anchor until the next nightly backup instead of comparing two unrelated chains (found in review the same day); someone able to rebuild the whole history with a newer first event therefore gets this WARN, not a FAIL. What it does not prove: someone with superuser rights in the database and access to the host could alter both the history and the backup folder, and a change between two backups is seen only at the next one. iamcatalog (Database catalog): FAIL on any object of medcea, medcea_auth, iam_policy or iam not owned by medcea_owner, any protective trigger (the iam freeze and append-only triggers, the append-only, no-truncate and retired-guard triggers, user_unit_audit_trg, commissioning_history_trg) not ENABLE ALWAYS, and any medcea view without security_invoker, with the exact statements of tests/iam-db.sh (a test compares the two texts); one read-only query, counts and the first five object names. Adapted from the test fixture: the fixture's trigger counts are not checked (they pin the fixture's build), so a dropped trigger is not seen, only a disabled one; iamgrants does not see it either (it compares only the iam_ guard triggers of medcea). Also: tests/iam-hosts.sh asks kubectl for managedFields explicitly, the fix the first round made in the health check. apply.sh's nine checks are unchanged. Decided by the platform owner on 9 November 2026. Run on the live platform on 10 November 2026 (exercise E32, commit 0133421): 64 checks, 63 OK; History chain anchor and Database catalog OK on their first live run; Account drift WARNed one unrecorded account (no unexplained role: the admin role is explained by the seed fact ./deploy-infra.sh recorded that morning): the demo account viewer, which admin deactivated the same morning (decision 19; see the test accounts), after which Account drift was OK with 0 unrecorded accounts.The first round proved the applied policy is in force; it did not prove that the people in Keycloak are the ones the record says, that the history was not shortened, or that the database's protections were not switched off. The drift was visible only to someone who opened the Decisions tab; computing it in the background keeps the health check read-only (it mints no token and reads no names) and the counts carry nothing personal into the logs. Exempting only seeded accounts keeps the rule simple and makes every other account explain itself once. The anchor is the only copy of the head outside the database, so it catches a cut or rewritten history that verify_chain() alone cannot see (a shortened chain still verifies). The catalog's statements were proven on the fixture; using the same text keeps one definition of what "protected" means.
Nightly backups to a local folder (1 November 2026)One CronJob (apps/backup), daily at 02:30 UTC: pg_dump in custom format of the platform database and Keycloak's, the roles without passwords, and a copy of every AI workbench home, Node-RED's /data and Grafana's volume, into one dated folder per run in BACKUP_DIR on the host (default /var/backups/medcea, mode 700), with sizes, SHA-256 checksums and an OK marker written last. Folders older than BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS (14) are deleted after a good run, never the newest complete one. No uninstall deletes the folder. The health check warns after 26 hours without a complete backup and fails after 72. The restore is a documented, manual procedure (./apps/backup/backups.sh restore-help); no script runs it. Decided by the platform owner on 1 November 2026.Nothing backed up the workbench homes, Grafana's database or Node-RED's data, and the databases only through a manual export; the owner wants a copy from which a person's lost work or the whole platform can come back. A local folder needs no other service or credential; on its own disk it survives a reinstall and the mistakes it guards against, and the owner can point it at another disk. The restore stays manual because it stops services and drops databases, and what to put back (one home, or everything after a reinstall) is a decision a script cannot take safely. The job reads the volumes' whole directory read-only rather than each volume, so a new person's home is copied from its first night without a redeploy. Same host and disk is listed as a known gap. Exercise E12 in the training chapter checks a backup and a restore.
Unit assignment in the User Manager (12 November 2026)Reverses owner decision 4 of IAM 4.1 (units stay in units.sh): an admin assigns and removes an operator's units in the account's Units section, through the access service's database function iam.record_unit_decision; an assignment still waits for a qa person who is neither maker nor subject, and a removal applies at once. The owner's choices: both routes are admin only (K on unit assignments; at first qa and auditor were to read an account's units too, reversed the same day, see below); an assignment to an account that is not an operator, is disabled or has no person_id is refused with the reason, while removing a leftover unit stays allowed for any account; units.sh stays as the host and break-glass path (--bootstrap, an account Keycloak no longer has). The two routes widen the skeleton, so the change ships as an approved skeleton version. After the review the owner made the read route admin only (12 November 2026): the first proposal gave qa and auditor the read route, so it widened qa's own reach, and the approval rule refuses an approver whose role, or a role it includes, gains reach; only qa approves policy versions, so it could never have been approved. qa still sees every unit decision in the Decisions tab. Who may see an account's permissions stays open. The general consequence: under the current approval rule, no change that widens qa's own reach (or auditor's, which qa includes) can be approved by qa. The owner also kept two points as built: a production_manager counts as an operator and may be assigned units, although they already work in every unit; an administrator may assign a unit to a second account of their own person, since the qa person who confirms must be neither maker nor subject. Evidence: applied as skeleton version 3 on 12 November 2026 (proposed from commit 18bec35, approved by qa_user); exercise E2 the same day: decision 3 assigned UNIT01 to oper and qa_user confirmed it (history events 38 and 39), an assignment to the engineer account was refused (409, nothing recorded), and decision 4 removed it at once (event 40).Assigning units on the host made the administrator's claim of who they are (--by) unprovable, so every such row needed a qa attestation and the work needed host access. In the User Manager the maker is the signed-in administrator, the reason is required, and dual control is the same as for every other account decision. Refusing a non-operator, a disabled account or one without a person keeps assignments that could never take effect, or could not be tied to a person, out of the record; qa and auditor check what they confirm and review in the Decisions tab.
The Configuration UI follows the database's own answer (12 November 2026)No policy change, no new route, no skeleton version: only the page changes. Panels read with error-driven reads: a panel whose main read the database refuses (42501) says in plain words that the role does not read it; a secondary read (control algorithms in the Recipe ↔ Unit grid, device counts in the Zones panel) may fail and the panel shows less, with a note. Write controls follow one zero-row write probe per table the page writes (a PATCH naming a record that does not exist, sent once when the page opens): where the database refuses it, New, Edit, Import, the grid's grant and settings buttons, Copy, Retire, Save to Platform Library and Onboard Device are hidden, not greyed out; a read-only record opens with View. Any other answer keeps today's behaviour (the control shows and the database decides). Constraint refusals (drafts only, approved recipes only, existing slots) and the platform library's route-gate refusals keep coming at save time, now in plain words. A device import carries no zone, so maintenance's device import is always refused by the existing-slot rule, with a sentence saying so: the probe cannot tell a constrained right from a full one, so the button stays. A probe that does not answer within 4 seconds counts as unknown, and the controls stay invisible until the probes have answered. Exercise E33. Open items found, not fixed here: the scheduler's GET /api/units shows the number of allowed recipes and learned-state records to roles that read neither recipes nor controller state (admin, maintenance, qc, qp), a scheduler or policy change; the grid's Permission Settings still writes the legacy algorithm_id and algorithm_params columns, not a parameter set (params_id, migration 008).The owner asked for a fix now, without a policy change. The database stays the only decider and the page needs no role list, so it cannot drift from the policy; under IAM_DB_ROLES=false the answer is truthful too (every person runs with the same grants, so every person sees the same buttons). Rejected: the PostgREST OpenAPI root (it lists write operations from the table's structure, not the role's privileges, so admin would still see Edit on units); a medcea.my_privileges() function (granted to every role it widens qa's own reach, which qa cannot approve); a compiled capabilities document (a new compile target, digest and health work, the policy's intent rather than the database's answer, and wrong under IAM_DB_ROLES=false); asking PostgREST to roll back each probe (needs a config-api setting that lets any client roll back). Hiding is a convenience for the person, never the control. Cost: about ten extra requests per page load and one "permission denied" line in the PostgreSQL log per refused probe. Evidence: exercise E33 run on 13 November 2026 (commit 27a5c2b) with admin, eng and qa_user, each offered only what the database accepts; the PostgreSQL log shows ten refused write questions for admin and qa, one (recipe_unit_permission) for engineer.
Feedback control: the control loop table for the runner only, the engineer's path as its own skeleton version (Q19, 13 November 2026)Version 2a (proposed from commit d8a91f8): medcea.control_loop is a member of master_data with service_only: [svc_scheduler] and written_by: functions, so the runner's account reads it and no person role gains anything. Version 2c (proposed from commit af5c1ad): the functions medcea.zone_loop_context(integer) and medcea.save_zone_loops(integer, jsonb) join master_data at level U, right after unit_commissioning(); only engineer holds U there, so it widens engineer alone (two EXECUTE rights) and bars only engineer from approving. Two versions, two qa approvals (choice D-e). The table is written only through save_zone_loops (SECURITY DEFINER, with the person's own sign-in; replace-all; refused while the unit has a run running or scheduled); migration 010 creates both functions without any grant, and only version 2c grants them. Rows are stamped with the person and every change goes to medcea.row_change (the 15th attributed table); a master-data review by qa (medcea.approve_change) covers them like any master data. Evidence: pending the rollout (nothing of Phases 1 and 2 is deployed yet; the rollout is in Rollout of Phases 1 and 2, the exercises are E34 to E36).The owner's answer to Q1 (master_data, engineer changes, qa reviews, the runner reads) could not be approved as one version: a plain master_data member gives every role holding R there a read, so qa's and auditor's reach would widen, and the approval rule refuses an approver whose own role (or a role it includes) gains reach; only qa approves policy versions. Keeping the table service-only and giving people only the two functions widens nobody but the writers, and splitting the two steps keeps each version approvable by qa. One version holding both was possible only with Q19 worded otherwise.
Feedback control: the reference sensor is always the person's choice in onboarding (Q20, 13 November 2026)Which sensor a loop is controlled on (a reference with an optional fallback, or the mean, lowest or highest of several) is chosen in the onboarding wizard's loop picker, which ships in this release (Phase 6's picker, command mode only): during an onboarding, on the tile Control loops of a zone, or with flash-device.sh --loops-only. One sensor on a reading is preselected; with several nothing is, and the row stays in error until the person chooses, or unticks the quantity (not controlled). Decide later writes nothing; Stop all loops needs a confirmation. A zone without loop rows runs on the default map, decided zone by zone (choice D-a): a reading with exactly one fresh sensor uses it; several give no data and the alarm ambiguous_source in the run log, never a guess. Evidence: pending the rollout (nothing of Phases 1 and 2 is deployed yet; the rollout is in Rollout of Phases 1 and 2, the exercises are E34 to E36).The owner differed from the recommended priority list: a fixed order would make the platform pick a sensor nobody chose, and the choice of reference is part of how the chamber is controlled. With the picker in the same release, the choice can be made the day the second sensor appears; until it is, the run says so instead of mixing readings (an SCD30 that heats itself would have biased a mean).
Feedback control Phases 1 and 2: the owner's earlier answers this release implements (12 November 2026)Of the owner's answers of 12 November 2026 (the feedback control plan's questions Q1 to Q18), this release implements: Q1 as reworded by Q19 (above); Q8, partly: a stale reference hands over to the fallback with the alarm fallback_in_use; with no fresh source the loop holds its last command with the alarm no_fresh_data and never switches the fans off for lack of data; alarms are run log lines (the e-mail of Q8 is Phase 9, Q18); Q11: the default map for zones without loop rows reads ground_temperature for the substrate (defect F1) and turns the fans UP when CO2 is above its limit, through the fixed command map DOWN→UP, UP→OFF, OFF→OFF (defect F11), with a health WARN (controlloops); Q12: Phases 1 and 2 are deployed together, and both topic forms are accepted (sense/<tag>/<sensor>, and the old sense/<tag> as sensor default); Q13: the SCD30's temperature and humidity are on by default, also in the two shipped board templates. From the owner's review of the loop mapping (11 November 2026): D1, the choice of sensor runs on the server, in the runner, while the board keeps turning commands into pins; D2, the sensor is identified by an extra topic level plus a sensor field in the message; D4, the loops are a table, read once when a run starts and copied into every cycle's run parameters (control_loops, control_loops_source), so the record shows which loops the run used, and a restarted run warns when its completed cycles ran other loops. The other answers (Q2 to Q7, Q9, Q10, Q14 to Q18) belong to later phases. Not yet (until Phase 4, Q3): an in-range OFF from the algorithm and the end of a run still switch the fans off. Evidence: pending the rollout (nothing of Phases 1 and 2 is deployed yet; the rollout is in Rollout of Phases 1 and 2, the exercises are E34 to E36).Recorded so that the behaviour of a run can be traced to the owner's answer it follows, and so that what is still open (Q8 in full, Q3) is not mistaken for done.
Feedback control: choices taken as recommended, pending the owner's override (13 November 2026)D-a: the default map is decided per zone (a zone with loop rows uses them, a zone without rows gets the default map), not per unit. D-b: no picker under IAM_DB_ROLES=false: the anonymous role gets no right on the two functions, and the wizard says "control loops can be chosen only with IAM_DB_ROLES=true". D-c: maintenance gets no read of the loops; re-onboarding by maintenance skips the picker with a sentence naming the engineer's command. D-d: flash-device.sh --loops-only (and its medcea.sh entry and wizard tile) is in this release. D-e: two skeleton versions (above). Evidence: pending the rollout (nothing of Phases 1 and 2 is deployed yet; the rollout is in Rollout of Phases 1 and 2, the exercises are E34 to E36).Each was the recommendation of the mapping of 13 November 2026, taken so that the work could go on; the owner may override any of them in the phase report. D-a keeps a unit with one zone already chosen from losing control of its other zones; D-b avoids a grant to the anonymous role; D-c widens nothing that qa would have to approve, and maintenance cannot re-onboard under IAM_DB_ROLES=true anyway (a known gap); D-d gives a way to change loops after a refusal during a run without flashing a board again.
Feedback control Phases 1 and 2: deviations from the plan (13 November 2026)The Run Monitor shows the latest value per zone, reading and sensor (the plan said per reading and sensor; a unit may have several zones). Grafana shows every sensor, one series per zone and sensor, not only the loop's reference (no loops are chosen yet, and a dashboard would otherwise depend on each zone's choice); its summary table now shows the latest value, where it showed the highest in the time range. Alarm cadence: an alarm line when a loop enters the state, the same line every 300 seconds while it lasts, and ALARM_CLEARED when it ends. E_TAG_DUP narrowed, not removed: two sensors may publish one reading, one sensor may not publish two of its readings on one reading (it would put two series on one topic). A reserved sensor id: default, the name of the sensor of a reading from an old board, is refused on the wiring screen (E_ID_RESERVED). Rules the database, the wizard and the runner share: the four loops and their recipe limits (air humidity on hr_lower_limit/hr_upper_limit, substrate on ground_temperature), command mode only, one loop per actuator, a maximum age of 1 to 3600 whole seconds, CO2's fixed command map. A recipe step with no limit for a loop leaves the loop inactive with a warning; loop rows the runner cannot use fail the run at its start, before anything is written. Evidence: pending the rollout (nothing of Phases 1 and 2 is deployed yet; the rollout is in Rollout of Phases 1 and 2, the exercises are E34 to E36).Each follows from a check of the plan against the code (13 November 2026) or from the owner's answers above; listed here because they differ from what the plan said.
Recipe types as master templates (15 November 2026)A recipe has a recipe type, Plants or Fungi, which lists the quantities its steps set, each required or optional; the quantities (unit, sense units, default tag, actuator commands, command map, phase, whether a loop exists, plausible range) and the types are one file in git, apps/database/recipe_types.yaml, which every database deploy seeds into medcea.control_quantity, medcea.recipe_type and medcea.recipe_type_quantity (migration 011). The loop codes are the quantity codes and are never renamed. Asked for by the platform owner on 15 November 2026.Each loop code was tied to two fixed recipe columns and the same four-entry table was copied in the database, the runner and the wizard, so a new controlled value needed a column and every copy changed; onboarding could not know what a unit needs. With the catalogue a new quantity is data. Git as the editor keeps every change reviewed and in the history; a quantity in use cannot be removed (the deploy stops on the foreign key).
A step's limits are one map, not a table (15 November 2026)recipe_line.setpoints holds {"<quantity>": {"lower": …, "upper": …}} for the quantities of the recipe's type; a trigger refuses a quantity the type does not list, a value outside its range and a lower limit above the upper; approving a recipe needs every required quantity on every step. The eight limit columns are read-only from migration 011 and are dropped by migration 012. The catalogue tables are read by the runner's account only, and people get the same file as static JSON. Owner decision of 15 November 2026, on the reviewer's finding.The owner asked for one row per value. A table every recipe reader could read would widen qa's own reach, and the approval rule refuses an approver whose own role gains access, so the version could never be applied (the dead end the User Manager's units met on 12 November 2026). A column moves no privilege; the existing draft, approval, digest and change-log triggers cover it as they cover every step column.
A unit's type is its recipe type (15 November 2026)cea_unit.unit_type holds a recipe type code (Greens became PLANT, Mushrooms FUNGI; migration 011 refuses a unit of any other label, naming it). A recipe may be permitted, scheduled and run only on a unit of its type: a policy refusal, a warning while IAM_DB_ROLES is false and refused once it is true. A recipe's type is fixed once it has steps. Asked for by the platform owner on 15 November 2026.The unit's label was free text nothing read. Making it the recipe type gives the onboarding wizard the quantities a zone's loops are for, and keeps a fungi recipe off a plant chamber.
Control loops bound half by half, in any order (15 November 2026)A loop's input (sensor and tag) is bound by the SENSE board's onboarding, its output (actuator) by the CONTROL board's, in either order; --loops-only binds both. A SENSE reading feeds a quantity when its unit is one of the quantity's (any tag, not only the default one); a CONTROL actuator can declare the quantity it acts on in its channel map. Asked for by the platform owner on 15 November 2026.The picker appeared only at a zone's second board, so the order of onboarding decided whether loops were chosen at all. Each person now chooses what their own board brings, and the zone's loops follow the unit's recipe type.
A half-bound loop runs on the default map's other half (implementation choice, 15 November 2026, awaiting the owner)The plan said a loop runs only once both halves are bound. As built, a run completes a half-bound loop with the default map's other half (the actuator declaring the quantity, else the one named after it; or every sensor of the quantity's default tag, one fresh one used), with a warning in the run log and in the health check's Control loops, and the cycle's run parameters mark the half taken. A loop with a sensor and no actuator in a zone that has no actuator for its quantity is not run (nothing would listen to the command), with a warning. The onboarding wizard says the same when it saves a half.Under the strict rule, a zone whose CONTROL board was onboarded before 15 November 2026 would lose all control the moment its SENSE board binds an input: the zone would have loop rows, so no default map, and no row with both halves. Completing with the default is what the zone ran before anyone chose. The owner may still choose the strict rule; it is a small change in the runner.
One policy version, relaxed enforcement during the build, approvals at the end (15 November 2026)The recipe types ship as one skeleton version (version 6, proposed from commit 32f0264: the catalogue for the runner only, nobody barred from approving it). During the build IAM_ENFORCE and then IAM_DB_ROLES are set false, so the draft, approved-only and recipe type rules only warn; at the end Bring IAM to full enforcement turns both back on and a qa person approves every recipe again, since migration 011 changed each one's approval digest. No approval is carried over by the migration. Owner decision of 15 November 2026 ("skip approvals and then enforce after the plan execution is complete").The changes touch the database, the runner, the Configuration UI, the Run Monitor and onboarding at once; approving every intermediate step would not review more. A widening of the skeleton cannot be skipped (every deploy refuses it, break-glass included), so it is the one version up front.
Deviation: enforcement relaxed for the recipe types build (16 November 2026, 08:15 to 21:43 UTC)IAM_ENFORCE false from 08:15 UTC and IAM_DB_ROLES false from 08:36; IAM_ENFORCE true again from 21:39 and IAM_DB_ROLES from 21:43 (history events 73 to 76), through Bring IAM to full enforcement; the services' copy of IAM_ENFORCE followed with ./deploy-apps.sh --all a few minutes later, and the health check passed all 65 checks. In the window: migrations 011 and 012 deployed, two Fungi draft recipes written by eng, one run of one of them started by qa_user that failed at its start (UNIT01 has no CONTROL board yet). After it, qa_user approved one recipe and returned the other (E37). While relaxed, the services log "would refuse" instead of refusing, the database runs every person as the anonymous role with the pre-Phase 2 grants and only warns on policy refusals; nothing is approved in that window.The owner's decision above. The health check WARNs on both switches for the length of the window, and the hash chain records enforcement_disabled and enforcement_enabled with their times.
Research sandbox: the whole sandbox (16 November 2026)Build the whole Research Sandbox of the reference architecture (version 2, section 4), components RS.1 to RS.8: the pseudonymised data lake, the plant and biological twins, the simulation harness, the optimisation engine, the agent harness, the candidate registry with its promotion gateway and the validation vault, in eight phases (Not built yet). Its output is only ever proposed; a candidate reaches a chamber only as a draft a qa person approves. Owner decision of 16 November 2026.The thesis's experiments need controllers and recipes tried before they reach a chamber, and the evidence for each candidate kept with it. Doing it inside the platform's own services would let research code touch regulated records; a separate zone with one gateway keeps the operational side as it is.
Research sandbox: a hosted model and a local model, chosen per agent session (16 November 2026)The agent harness offers both a hosted model (Claude, through an API) and a local model on the host's CPUs, behind one model interface, and each agent session says which it uses (open point OP2). The hosted model's egress is its own phase, with its own decision record (Phase 5). Owner decision of 16 November 2026.The host has no GPU, so a local model is small and slow but keeps everything on the host; the hosted model is stronger but sends prompts out. Choosing per session lets a campaign whose prompts must stay on the host use the local model.
Research sandbox: our own minimal agent loop (16 November 2026)The agent harness's loop (prompt, tool call, result, next step) is our own minimal Python code, not an agent framework (open point OP1). Owner decision of 16 November 2026.A short loop of our own can be read in full, tested offline and recorded step by step; a framework brings code and network calls nobody here reviewed.
Research sandbox: controller campaigns first (16 November 2026)The sandbox's first use is controller campaigns for the control_scientist: comparing and tuning on/off control (If-Then-Else), PID, FLC, MPC and Q-learning on the chamber model by distance from the band's middle, time spent next to an edge and energy, to prepare Experiment 1 (May 2027). Phase 1 makes a campaign run by hand on the host (Running a campaign, exercise E39); a supervised agent runs one from Phase 4. Owner decision of 16 November 2026.Experiment 1 compares these controllers on the chambers; a campaign on a model first shows which settings are worth the chamber time, and finds defects before a run does (it found the two below). Run on 17 November 2026 (exercise E39, commit a175c52): the same spec gave the same result digest twice, PID moved with the clock's origin, and every FLC and MPC run without its library was marked invalid.
Research sandbox: loosely coupled, data by snapshot only (17 November 2026)The sandbox is its own application, coupled to the rest of MedCEA through four interfaces only (the coupling contract): identity shared (the realm, the roles, the access policy's route table); data by snapshot, never a live connection to the operational database: an exporter in the platform's namespace reads read-only research views and writes immutable snapshots into the research database (Phase 3); metadata read from production's own sources at a pinned commit, never copied (the quantity catalogue, recipe format 2 and its setpoint rules, the controller interface, codes and parameter schemas, the loop rules, the CONTROL board's command semantics); candidates out through one gateway that runs production's checks and writes only a draft (Phase 6). Nothing else is shared. Asked for by the platform owner on 17 November 2026: "ensure the research sandbox is loosely coupled from the rest of MedCEA applications, it shared the IAM, accesses the database to reach to measurements, etc and any metadata that is required to make the control model and recipies produced compatible"; the snapshot rule is the owner's decision of the same day.A live connection would put research code, and later agents, one query away from regulated data and from the platform's load; a snapshot is pseudonymised, numbered and immutable, so a campaign names the data it used. Reading the metadata from production's sources, never a copy, keeps what the sandbox produces compatible with what the platform will accept: the same rules judge it on both sides.
MPC's command sign fixed and its libraries installed in the scheduler (17 November 2026)What was wrong. schd/cea/algorithms/mpc.py answered UP for a negative solver output and DOWN for a positive one, while in its own model a positive output raises the reading: below its band MPC answered DOWN (cool), above it UP (heat). Production never ran it: the scheduler pod did not install GEKKO, so MPC always fell back, silently, to on/off control; FLC did the same without scikit-fuzzy, and would have even with it, because scikit-fuzzy 0.5.0 needs packaging without declaring it. The fix: a positive output above the dead band is UP, a negative one DOWN; FLC and MPC count every fallback with its reason and write a WARNING flc fallback / WARNING mpc fallback line (the first, then at most one an hour); the scheduler pod installs GEKKO 1.3.3, scikit-fuzzy 0.5.0, numpy, scipy, networkx and packaging, each pinned by version and checksum (apps/scheduler/requirements-controllers.txt); the health check Controller libraries warns while they are missing. Choosing MPC or FLC for a unit, a new parameter set for either, or any further change to their code goes to qa as before. Deployed with ./apps/scheduler/deploy.sh only while no run is active (the restart installs the libraries and would end a running runner). Evidence: pending the deploy (exercise E40). Fix approved by the platform owner on 17 November 2026, before the libraries were installed.Installing GEKKO first would have made every MPC run drive its chamber away from the band. With the sign fixed, the libraries make MPC and FLC run their own code for the first time; the fallback lines and the health check make a fallback visible instead of silent, and the sandbox marks a run that fell back invalid (The simulation harness). Deployed on 17 November 2026 (commit a175c52, no run active; exercise E40 steps 1–2): Controller libraries OK with the pinned versions, and MPC and FLC answered without a fallback in the pod; a run on a unit waits for a CONTROL board.
The portal by data zone, the manual in the user menu (17 November 2026)The portal's main page has four areas, grouped by where their data comes from: Operations (Run Monitor, Recipe Schedule Manager, System Configuration; live data), Reports (Grafana's standard reports and Superset's ad-hoc analysis; live data), Research workbench (the AI Workbench's notebooks, later agent campaigns and a Superset on snapshots) and Platform Management (administration). Each area's page says in one line what data its apps work on. The Monitor, the Scheduler and the Configuration UI left Platform Management, where they were mislabelled as administration. Grafana is the tool for standard reports: dashboards provisioned from git (apps/report/dashboards/), nobody saves over them in the browser. The Platform manual card is gone; the manual is linked from the user menu of every signed-in app, between Profile and Sign out, at the portal's address. The portal still shows every card to every role; each app's gate decides (no change to the access policy). The Notebooks card is greyed out where WORKBENCH_ENABLED=false. Decided by the platform owner on 17 November 2026.A user and an auditor need to know whether an app works on live operational data or on the research sandbox's snapshots more than which tool it is, and the zone is what the research rules depend on. Documentation sits where platforms usually put it, in the account menu, and is then one click away from every app, not only from the portal. Grafana's dashboards are reviewed through git, which makes it the controlled channel for reports everyone reads.
Research sandbox: Phase 2 in two steps, and the notebooks' live sign-in disabled (17 November 2026)The snapshot export is built before the AI Workbench moves: Phase 2a builds the research database, the held-out reservation, the research views and the pseudonymised export while the Workbench keeps reading live data; Phase 2b moves the Workbench into the research sandbox and switches medcea_data.py from live reads to snapshots in the same deploy, under the same names (md.measurements(...)), with the example notebooks rewritten. Phase 3 is the calibration of the chamber model. At 2b the Keycloak client workbench-notebook, through which a notebook reads the configuration API as the person, is disabled, not deleted: ./deploy-infra.sh stops re-enabling it, it leaves the platform's client lists, and a check proves it stays disabled; deleting it is a later decision. The research sandbox's notebooks also lose the route to the platform's addresses through the Tailscale range (100.64.0.0/10), which their network policy did not exclude. Decided by the platform owner on 17 November 2026.Notebooks are never without data: they switch from live reads to snapshots in one step. A snapshot can be named in a result and read again a year later, carries no names or account ids, and leaves out the data kept back for the final validation (RS.8); a live read does none of that. Disabling first keeps the client's id and its history, and a later decision can delete it.
Research sandbox: who administers the AI Workbench (D1, 17 November 2026)The admin role keeps K on the AI Workbench and stays its hub administrator (the admin page, stopping a server, removing a person from the hub at offboarding, after their platform account is deactivated), but gets no workspace: from Phase 2b the hub refuses to start a notebook server for an account whose only Workbench right is administration. Invariant I18 is written with that K exempt from the start. A health warning lists hub accounts without an enabled platform account, because their personal hub tokens outlive the account. Built in Phase 2b; no access policy change for this decision. Decided by the platform owner on 17 November 2026 (option A2).The thesis's RBAC specification gives the system administrator K (configure, no data) on the sandbox; its role-to-component mapping keeps the administrator out of the Workbench. Administration without a workspace satisfies both: offboarding stays in the browser under a named person, and no administrator session can run code in the research zone, which is the compensating control for one person holding several roles on this prototype.
Research sandbox: live data for the scientists, Superset, the engineer and qa (17 November 2026)At the Phase 2b switchover: bio_scientist and control_scientist lose their live read of measurements (the Run Monitor and the Configuration UI's measurement queries) and their Superset; production_manager, qc and qp lose Superset and keep Grafana as viewers. The live Superset ends then; the engineer's dashboard is exported first. A Superset on snapshots in the research sandbox comes only when a scientist account needs it. In the research sandbox the engineer reads only, with one exception: importing a promoted candidate (the gateway, Phase 6); it is not a developer of the chamber model. qa keeps reading in the notebooks, so it can reproduce a scientist's analysis. All of these are narrowings, approved by qa as change versions. Deviations from the thesis, recorded: the scientists have no live dashboards (L3.6 becomes N for R8 and R9 on live data; their dashboards are the research sandbox's); the auditor has no Workbench access (the role-to-component mapping gives it R). Decided by the platform owner on 17 November 2026.Data kept back for the final validation is unseen only if nobody who develops a model can read it live: closing the notebooks alone would leave Superset's SQL Lab and the configuration API's full history open to the scientists, and the engineer's live tools (Grafana Explore, Node-RED, the MQTT Explorer) if the engineer were a model developer. The held-out reservation is therefore effective from the 2b switchover, not from the first snapshot.
No containerd restart on a running cluster (17 November 2026)What happened. ./deploy-infra.sh of 17 November 2026 restarted MicroK8s's containerd at its Docker Hub step: its check (two sudo greps) read a mistyped sudo password as "the credentials differ", rewrote certs.d/docker.io/hosts.toml unchanged and restarted containerd. On kernel 7.0.0-43 the running containers then kept MicroK8s's own AppArmor profile although the rules were loaded again within seconds; PostgreSQL's internal signals were refused, a planned restart of it hung and left the database unanswering for about 80 seconds (16:31–16:32 UTC; no run active, no data lost; readings that arrived then were refused, not stored), and the ingress controller and five sign-in proxies were refused the Go runtime's signals until restarted. What changed. The file is compared whole and written only when it differs, a refused sudo is reported and changes nothing, and containerd is never restarted for it (infra/lib-dockerhub.sh, also in the bootstrap): containerd 1.6.28 reads that file at every pull, and ignores its credentials table altogether, so image pulls from docker.io were and stay anonymous. Container AppArmor now names the pods still running that sent a refused signal, so the operator knows which to restart. Asked by the platform owner on 17 November 2026; the containerd behaviour was checked against containerd 1.6.28's source and documentation. Evidence: exercise E41, 18 November 2026 (training chapter, "Last done"): a refused sudo at that step printed "Nothing was restarted" and containerd's journal shows no restart; a deploy with the right password left the file "unchanged"; and the health check named the one pod still on the old profile from 17 November (deployment/hostpath-provisioner -n kube-system).Restarting containerd reaches every running container on the host, and on the newer kernels it silently weakens their confinement until each is restarted: a step that changes nothing must not cost that. The credentials in the file never worked, so not restarting loses nothing; whether to give containerd real Docker Hub credentials (its own configuration, which does need a restart) is left open, since no pull limit has been hit.
Research data carries no person, not even a pseudonym (18 November 2026)Nothing that names or stands for a person reaches the research sandbox: no creator, editor, executor or approver of anything, no account id, no name, and no pseudonym of any of them (no keyed hash, no pepper). The read functions the export uses return none (What the export reads, and never reads), and JSON is rebuilt from known keys so nothing a person typed passes through. Owner decision P of 18 November 2026.The sandbox's questions are about chambers, controllers and recipes, not about who ran them; a pseudonym would still be personal data, with a secret to keep and rotate, for no research use. With no person in the lake, the sandbox, its notebooks and later its agents hold no personal data at all. Exercise E42 (run 19 November 2026).
The export reads through owner-run read functions, EXECUTE only (18 November 2026)The exporter's login, svc_research_export, reads the operational database only through eleven functions medcea.research_*() (migration 013): owned by the database owner role, run with its rights, each with a fixed list of columns. It may only execute them and is refused on every table and view. The functions are created inert (nobody may execute them) and the access policy grants them to svc_research_export alone, through the group research_export of the skeleton version that follows. medcea.research_contract_version() (1) names the contract they implement; a change to a result column raises it. Owner decision F of 18 November 2026, in place of the research views first planned.A view over a base table gives its reader whatever the view's owner may read and grows silently when a column is added; a function's result is a stated contract, checked by tests for every forbidden column, and a grant of EXECUTE gives nothing else. The rehearsal of 18 November 2026 (a restore of that day's backup in a throwaway PostgreSQL) showed the export's login refused on the base tables.
The research lake is append-only, a snapshot is a high-water mark (18 November 2026)Each export adds one numbered snapshot up to a cut (the operational database's clock minus two minutes): the readings ingested since the previous cut, and whole copies of the small sets, with per-set row counts and sha256 digests (Snapshots and their digests). Nothing updates, deletes or truncates a lake table or a reservation, the research database's owner included; the triggers fire for replication sessions too. A snapshot is refused unless it follows the latest one. Owner decision S of 18 November 2026.A result can name the snapshot it was computed on and be recomputed from it later; the digests show the data is the same. A held-out row that never entered the lake cannot leak from it, and a row cannot be taken out of it to hide what a model saw. The research server's superuser can still disable a trigger; that is the host operator gap below.
The research database is outside the platform policy matrix; reservations are made by qa through a host command (18 November 2026)The research sandbox's PostgreSQL (medcea_research, in the research namespace) is not in the access policy's matrix and no person signs in to it. Its three roles and grants are written by hand (apps/research/db/grants.sql) and each deploy ends by checking them from the catalog (assert_grants.sql), stopping on any difference; its network is the research zone's compiled default-deny, checked by the health check Research network policies, and the snapshots by Research export. A held-out reservation is written by ./apps/research/reserve.sh add --by <qa username> on the host, which refuses an account that is not enabled or does not hold qa, and records its username and account id with the reason; it is not an account decision and not on the policy history. The review of 18 November 2026 found that the database chart's own NetworkPolicy (switched on by a key the first values file did not set) would have opened its port to the whole cluster; fixed before any deploy: it is switched off, the deploy refuses any NetworkPolicy in the zone the compile did not make, and the health check FAILs one. Implementation choice, 18 November 2026, under owner decisions P, F and S.The research database holds no regulated or personal data and serves no person directly in Phase 2a; putting it into the matrix would add policy approvals for a store only two service logins use. What protects the platform is in the matrix: the export's read on the operational side, and the zone's network. Reservations belong to qa, which owns the validation data; a host command keeps them out of every screen until the vault's own interface (Phase 7). --by is a claim the command checks against Keycloak but cannot prove, as for units.sh (known gaps). Evidence (19 November 2026, exercise E42). Reservation #1 by qa_user; snapshot 1 kept its 39,960 readings out (0 in the lake); a reservation named by eng was refused before anything was asked, and the database refused a range already exported; the research database pod could not reach the platform's PostgreSQL.
Research Phase 2a: where its code lives, and how it is switched on (18 November 2026)The research database's SQL and host commands live under apps/research/ (db/*.sql, reserve.sh), the exporter under apps/research-export/; research/ stays the sandbox's own code, which imports nothing from the platform. Only the research namespace is created in Phase 2a; the gateway namespace (<NAMESPACE>-research-gw) comes with its first pod in Phase 4. RESEARCH_ENABLED is off by default: until it is switched on (and the applied policy has the research zone), every research deploy prints one "skipped" line and changes nothing. The exporter runs in the research database's own image (its psql and a POSIX shell, as the backup job does): no Python, no extra packages. Implementation choices of 18 November 2026, recorded for the owner. Its default is superseded by O11(b) of 19 November 2026 (below): from Phase 2b RESEARCH_ENABLED is true in config.env.example.Keeping the sandbox's code apart keeps the coupling contract's isolation test as it is. A namespace with nothing in it would be a policy target with nothing to protect. Opt-in keeps an install that does no research free of the research database and its nightly job. The database image is already on the node and its psql matches the research server; a Python image would bring a wheel cache and a second set of pins.
Invariant I18: who may hold what on research groups (18 November 2026)A resource group marked zone: research is a research group. On research groups operator, production_manager, qp, maintenance and qc hold nothing, and engineer holds at most R; the one exception, kept for a group a later phase adds, is the promotion group, where the engineer holds R and C (importing a promoted candidate). The engineer works in research as an operational role only: it is not a developer of the chamber model, so it holds no C or U on a chamber model group either. The admin role's K on the AI Workbench (research_workbench) is allowed (decision D1 of 17 November 2026); the scientists and qa are not limited by I18. The checker (apps/iam/compiler/invariants.py) holds the rule now and has nothing to check until a group carries the zone; the rule's text enters the policy with the skeleton version that marks research_workbench as a research group. Under the owner's decisions of 17 November 2026 (D1, and the engineer reads only in research).The research zone is where models are developed on data kept from production; production roles have no reason to reach it, and a production role that could would make the separation of research from production depend on nobody using it. Writing I18 with the administrator's K exempt from the start avoids rewording an invariant later, which would itself widen the policy.
