Research Phase 2b: the AI Workbench moves into the research zone in one switchover (19 November 2026)Commit A (all code, the access policy unchanged: under the applied version 7 every compiled artefact stays byte for byte the same) is deployed first. Commit B, a skeleton version approved by qa, places the AI Workbench's hub, its proxy, the notebooks and the snapshot reader lake-api in the research zone and removes the notebooks' live path (client notebooks and its hop to the configuration API). Applying it and moving the workbench (./infra/deploy-workbench.sh --move) run under one lock; the apply records the workbench step as deferred until the move is done (Rollout of Phase 2b). Then a change version, drafted from the factory defaults, takes the narrowed cells. The move: home volumes set to Retain before anything is uninstalled; homes copied on the host with sudo cp -a; the hub's database starts fresh (hub users and their API tokens dropped); claim-admin not copied; the old claims kept, labelled, until the administrator removes them; the certificate workbench-tls issued for the workbench's address alone. Owner decisions of 19 November 2026 (accepted as recommended in the design and its review).One switchover keeps the window in which notebooks could read live data and also sit in the research zone at zero. Every new behaviour keys on what only the skeleton version adds, so commit A can be deployed and checked on its own. Nothing a person made is deleted by a script.
Research Phase 2b, commit B: what the skeleton version widens (checked offline, 19 November 2026)Commit B is written and checked offline, not yet proposed. Against commit A with version 7's cells the skeleton gate reports a widening of the system only: the four new zone pods' network paths (the hub, its proxy, the notebooks and lake-api, including the notebooks' internet path on TCP 443 and the hub's paths to Keycloak and to the cluster's API), lake-api's path to the research database, and as changed sections the pods' labels, zone and outgoing paths, the internet exception list, the AI Workbench's risk text and the removed notebooks client. No role's reach moves, the checker passes on version 7's cells, and no role is barred from approving it, so a qa person may. Invariant I19 is added; adding an invariant only tightens, so it is not counted as a widening. The change version that follows (the factory cells) only narrows six roles and widens none, so any qa person may approve it too. The diff the proposal stores (made with commit A's compiler) is the one apply.sh recomputes with commit B's, so an approved version is not refused at its apply for a compiler change (found in review: B first registered the zone pods' outgoing paths as reach, which would have moved the diff's sections; they stay residue). Evidence: tests/test_policy_source.py PhaseRS2bBDelta and tests/test_research_policy.py Phase2b; the proposal's own --check-only output is the live evidence once it runs.The approver sees beforehand exactly what the version opens, and the rule that no role may approve a widening of its own reach is checked before anything is proposed.
Skeleton version B of research Phase 2b is never rolled back; commit A cannot be reverted after it (19 November 2026)As Superset's version 15: --rollback-to keeps the accepted skeleton, so undoing 2b is a new skeleton version proposed from a git revert of B, approved by qa, applied, followed by ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh --move back (which copies the homes back, with the work done in the zone) and apply.sh --resume; ./deploy-infra.sh then enables workbench-notebook again because the policy names it. Commit A can be reverted only before B is applied. Owner decision of 19 November 2026.B's network forms (platform, node and internet hops) are refused by a checker without commit A, so after B a revert of A would stop every compile and every deploy, the host's policy file included.
The orchestrator is deferred to Phase 4 (O1, 19 November 2026)Phase 2b builds no orchestrator, no group research_campaigns, no research-agent client, no session tokens and no simulation Job template; no research service in the zone checks the route table yet, so the zone holds no copy of the route table or the realm's keys. Scientists run campaigns in their own notebook. The change version therefore adds no cell. Owner decision O1 of 19 November 2026.The orchestrator's design depends on the agent harness of Phase 4; building it twice would cost more than the wait.
Notebooks read the lake through a reader with no identity (O2, 19 November 2026)lake-api, a PostgREST in the research namespace over the read functions of schema lake_api, verifies no token and holds no credential of any person; no notebook holds a credential either. Only notebook pods and the host reach it (its compiled network policy), and its database login may only execute those functions, read-only, 30 seconds per statement, 10 connections. A recorded exception to the rule that every request goes through the route table (Phase 5, rule 4): here the database decides what is answered, not the route table. A consequence: any account on the platform host can read the lake through the host's own path to it (critique 22); the lake holds no person and nothing a person typed, so this is accepted. Who made a held-out reservation and why is never readable through it; the ranges themselves are readable (O4). Runs, cycles, control loops and parameter sets are not readable from notebooks before Phase 3 decides what is needed (O3). Owner decisions O2–O4 of 19 November 2026.Snapshots are person-free and the same for every scientist, so a per-person identity would protect nothing and would put a token back into the notebooks, which 2b takes out.
The engineer loses Superset too; no role keeps it (O12, 19 November 2026)The change version of Phase 2b removes bio_scientist's and control_scientist's Read on telemetry and every role's cell on analysis (the scientists', production_manager's, qc's, qp's and the engineer's), so Superset's gate-only deploy stops Superset (its database is kept and still backed up nightly); the engineer's dashboard is exported first. The factory defaults carry the same narrowed cells, with analysis: {} as an empty mapping (a checker error refuses a row that is not a mapping), so a fresh install has no Superset from then on. Owner decision O12 of 19 November 2026; supersedes "Superset installed by default" of 8 November 2026.Invariant I11 needs the scientists' analysis to go with their telemetry; once only the engineer was left, a live Superset for one role was not worth its upkeep. A Superset on snapshots comes when a scientist needs it.
The hub's rights in the research namespace: no Secrets, pod security baseline (19 November 2026)The hub runs on a Role of its own, medcea-hub: pods and volume claims (read, create, delete) and events (read), and no Secrets and no Services (services taken out in the review of 19 November 2026: KubeSpawner creates none here, and a NodePort the hub could create would open the snapshot reader, which admits the node, to the LAN) (KubeSpawner needs them only for internal TLS, which is off; to be confirmed live by exercise E43: a refusal on Secrets in the hub's log goes to the owner, never silently re-added). The research namespace enforces the pod security level baseline, which refuses a privileged pod, host networking or a host directory; the chart's metadata-blocking init container, which needs a network privilege, is switched off (the internet hop already excludes the link-local range). The same pod security gap exists today in the platform namespace, recorded in known gaps. The health check Research grants and Secrets FAILs a pod naming a Secret outside its list or a Role granting Secrets. Owner decision C of 19 November 2026.A hub that may create pods could otherwise create one that owns the machine; reading Secrets would give it every password in the namespace. Prevention is the pod security level; the health check is detection. Evidence (20 November 2026, exercise E43). The live Role names pods, volume claims and events only; the hub started bio_user's workspace and its log held no refusal on Secrets; Research grants and Secrets OK.
Notebook internet access: TCP 443, IPv4, the excluded ranges in the policy (19 November 2026)A notebook in the research zone reaches the internet on TCP port 443 only (package installs, GitHub over https, the VS Code download), over IPv4 (the network rule's address block is IPv4), never 10.0.0.0/8, 100.64.0.0/10 (Tailscale), 169.254.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12 or 192.168.0.0/16. The excluded ranges are written in the access policy (network.zones.research.internet_except), so changing them is a skeleton change that qa approves, and the policy checker refuses a list that leaves any of those five ranges out (added in the review of 19 November 2026, so that a mistaken approval cannot open the platform's database or the LAN; more ranges may be added). A router that sends the platform's own public address back inside (hairpin) is tested by tests/iam-research.sh --wan-ip; if it answers, its address is added to the list by a skeleton version. Owner decision D of 19 November 2026.Notebook work needs packages and git; private and Tailscale ranges would reach the platform's hosts through ingress. In the policy, the list is reviewed like any other widening.
Separation of duties for the AI Workbench: invariant I19 (SoD-3, 19 November 2026)On every resource group of the research zone the admin role holds nothing, except K (configure) on the AI Workbench; the checker refuses anything else once the skeleton version adds the invariant. With it the hub refuses to start a workspace for an account whose only workbench right is administration (decision D1 = A2 of 17 November 2026, effective with the move). Invariant I5's rationale still speaks of the live telemetry the scientists will no longer read; it is left word for word on purpose, because rewording an invariant counts as a widening of the skeleton. Evidence of D1 (20 November 2026, exercise E43). With version 8 applied, tests/iam-workbench.sh W10: admin opens the hub's admin page (200) and its own workspace is refused (403, "Administration of the AI workbench gives no workspace: sign in with an account whose role uses the workbench.").Administering the AI Workbench is not doing research in it (PIC/S PI 041-1 §9.3).
Removing the live tests' hub users (20 November 2026)At their end, tests/iam-workbench.sh and tests/iam-signin.sh remove from the AI Workbench's hub every user whose name has the throwaway form test-<role>-<6 hex>, that has no account in the realm any more and that has no workspace running. This catches the run's own throwaway administrator and any left by earlier runs. They do it in the hub's own database, the way the hub's "remove user" does, and then restart the hub, which takes about a minute: running workspaces keep running, and sign-ins wait. Any other hub user is never touched, and no home folder is touched. Both tests hold the deploy lock. Owner decision of 20 November 2026.JupyterHub refuses to let an account delete itself, and any second administrator used to remove the first becomes the next leftover. The alternatives were a standing hub token able to delete any hub user (a new credential) and sweeping earlier runs' leftovers only (one always remained, and so did the warning). Evidence (20 November 2026). tests/iam-workbench.sh passed W1–W10; at its end it removed test-admin-e0ce88 from the hub's database and the hub came back, and the next ./health-check.sh showed Workbench accounts OK.
A failed run is rerun as a new run or decommissioned for good (21 November 2026)On the owner's request: a Failed run offers ⟳ Rerun (a new run of the same recipe and unit, with a parameter set chosen in Run Now) and ⊘ Decommission, which keeps the run as a record and takes it out of use for good (is_active = 'N', through medcea.set_run_status(run, 'D'), level O like Stop, so the same people who may stop a run may decommission it). Against mistakes: the window enables its button only when the run's number is typed, the scheduler refuses a request that does not repeat it, and the database refuses every later transition and start_run of a decommissioned run. Retry stays for a run that carries a parameter set. No route, grant or policy change.Runs are never deleted (the Compliance Plane rule and the audit trail); a separate flag rather than a new status value keeps every reader of recipe_run_status unchanged. Exercise E52.
The online check falls back to a board's last reported address (20 November 2026)When the router cannot resolve a board's hostname, the Configuration page's Online check tries the address the board last reported in its own health or test message (a test message sent from the host is skipped), and shows a board that answers there amber, never green. platform-api's check now answers unresolved for a name that does not resolve, apart from a host that does not answer. A partial index measurement_status_idx (device and time, health and test messages only) keeps the lookup cheap; it is built concurrently by the database deploy. No policy change: the route GET /check/<host> is unchanged, and the address is read as the person through config-api, so while IAM_DB_ROLES is true a role that does not read measurements gets no fallback (before that, config-api answers every role as anon and every role gets it). A lookup of the name is bounded by the check's 3 s: only a definite no-such-name answer is unresolved, a stuck resolver is a timeout, so a router that stops answering never holds platform-api.Owner, 20 November 2026, after a CONTROL board onboarded under its new name stayed red because the router kept its old DHCP name. Amber, not green: the address may since belong to another machine. Evidence: exercise E46; tests/test_config_ui_online.py.
A custom domain without DNS records gets the platform's own name service (20 November 2026)For a custom domain configuration asks who answers DNS for it, with the platform itself (LOCAL_DNS="true") as the default and a DNS server elsewhere as the other answer; when Tailscale split DNS already sends the domain to this server it sets LOCAL_DNS="true" without asking. With Tailscale up it asks which address other devices use: the Tailscale one sets USE_TAILSCALE="true" and keeps the template's PLATFORM_IP line, the LAN one sets USE_TAILSCALE="false" and writes a PLATFORM_IP line that takes the LAN address. An existing config.env is never rewritten (a note says what to review). ./deploy-infra.sh checks that the platform's names resolve to this server, never fails on it, and lists it instead of SUCCESS; the readiness waits connect to PLATFORM_IP; ./install.sh closes with "Finished with problems" while the infrastructure listed a problem or the health check failed. Implementation choices awaiting the owner's confirmation: the default answer (the platform answers DNS itself), the question being skipped when Tailscale split DNS already routes the domain here, and the LAN-only PLATFORM_IP line.A fresh install on another server (20 November 2026) took DOMAIN="medcea.ai" with LOCAL_DNS="false" while Tailscale split DNS sent the domain to that server, where nothing answered on port 53: every lookup failed or hung, two readiness waits failed, and the install still said SUCCESS. The question was first planned as "do DNS records already point at this server?", which that operator would have answered yes (split DNS did point there) while the platform had to answer, hence "who answers". PLATFORM_IP was the Tailscale address while USE_TAILSCALE was false because the template's line prefers Tailscale whenever it is up; for a domain reached through Tailscale that is right (the name server must bind where split DNS sends the lookups), so the line is not changed for existing installs, only written for a LAN-only choice. Evidence: tests/test_domain_dns.py; exercise E47.
RESEARCH_ENABLED defaults to true; research off with the workbench placed in the zone (19 November 2026)A new config.env has RESEARCH_ENABLED="true" (owner decision O11(b)); an existing one keeps its value, and one from before 18 November 2026 that has no such line is given "false" by infra/configure.sh, with a note (review of 19 November 2026: it ran without the research sandbox, and switching it on is the owner's decision). When the policy places the workbench in the research zone and RESEARCH_ENABLED is not true, the deploys install nothing and leave a running hub alone with a warning; a full install into the zone refuses unless the zone's compiled network policies are in place. Owner decision O11(b) of 19 November 2026; the second sentence is an implementation choice, recorded for the owner.From Phase 2b the AI Workbench lives in the research zone, so a platform without the zone has no workbench. Stopping or uninstalling a hub because a switch is off would end people's work without warning.
The notebooks' live sign-in client is disabled, not created (19 November 2026)Keycloak client workbench-notebook exists only while the applied policy names it as a notebook client: ./deploy-infra.sh no longer creates it on a fresh install once B is applied, and disables an existing one (never deletes it); the move does the same. The health check Keycloak client scopes FAILs it while it is present and enabled after that. Owner decision of 17 November 2026 (D2), as built.A disabled client keeps its configuration and its history in Keycloak for an audit; a deletion is a later decision.
Research Phase 3: build now, fit what's there (20 November 2026)The whole calibration pipeline is built: snapshots fetched by their lineage and checked against their recorded digests, fits that say what a dataset can identify, scenarios pinned to a calibration file and to a snapshot's recipe step, and manifests that name both. The sensor model is calibrated now, from snapshot 1 (UNIT01/ZONE01, lineage 096015bc…). The plant constants stay flagged assumptions. A step-test protocol is written for when a CONTROL board is fitted (The step-test protocol), and the two controller comparisons are run again on the calibrated model (The comparisons on the calibrated model). Nothing writes the lake, the access policy does not change and nothing is deployed. Owner decision of 20 November 2026; it supersedes the plan's "the time constant, humidity and CO2 constants are calibrated from the lake's measurements".The lake holds 14 hours of readings of one chamber with nothing switching in it: enough to describe the sensors, not the plant. Building the pipeline now means the plant can be fitted as soon as step-test data exists, and the comparisons already run on what the boards really publish (a reading every 3 seconds, not 30). Evidence (20 November 2026, exercise E45). Snapshot 1 fetched twice with identical files, its measurement digest recomputed from 83,353 readings; the committed calibration reproduced; the comparisons run with 0 invalid runs and the same result digest at one and at several processes.
Plant constants are refused until there is excitation (20 November 2026)python3 -m research.calib fit-plant refuses every plant constant but the volume, writes nothing and exits 3 while no dataset shows an actuator switching against a measured room (codes NO_ACTUATOR_DATA, NO_EXCITATION, NO_AMBIENT, and for some constants NOT_OBSERVED, CONDITIONAL_REFUSED, LITERATURE). A calibration file with a fitted plant value is refused in Phase 3, and so is one whose assumed value differs from the model's. The lake's export contract (version 1) carries readings only; the change that adds the boards' state reports and the commands (two read functions, contract version 2, a lake table and a reader function) is deferred to a later phase, with its own skeleton version for qa to approve. Owner decision of 20 November 2026.A constant fitted from readings alone would be a guess with a number on it: without knowing when the heater ran, the time constant and the heat capacity cannot be told apart from the room's drift. Evidence (exercise E45). fit-plant on snapshot 1: exit 3, "no plant constant is identifiable from this dataset; nothing written".
The SCD30 is calibrated relative to the SHT45, with its humidity model chosen (20 November 2026)The SHT45 is the reference sensor: offsets are fitted for the SCD30 relative to it (+2.04 °C and −7.03 %RH on snapshot 1), never absolute. How the humidity offset is modelled is a choice recorded in the calibration file (humidity_model): constant_offset (two constant offsets), the default and the one committed, or self_heating (the SCD30 warms itself by 2.04 °C and sees the same water at a higher temperature, plus a remaining humidity offset). Both models' predictions at 50, 70, 85 and 95 %RH are in the file. The fit saw 51.35 to 55.33 %RH only; a scenario outside that range must state why the values may be used there (extrapolate), and the manifest repeats the reason. Implementation choice of 20 November 2026 (design review), recorded for the owner.The SHT45 has the better datasheet accuracy and the SCD30 warms itself; the loops already use the SHT45 as reference and the SCD30 as fallback. Self-heating explains only about a third of how the measured offset changes with humidity (slope −0.30 observed, −0.11 predicted), so neither model is proven by this data; the constant offset is the simpler one, and it matches the data at the humidity it was fitted on.
Runs, cycles, control loops and parameter sets stay unreadable through the lake reader (O3, 20 November 2026)Phase 3 does not expose them in lake-api. The calibration needs only measurements, recipes, recipe steps and the catalogue, which are readable; the lake holds no cycles and no control loops yet. Exposing them is a change to lake_api.sql (outside the access policy's matrix, not a skeleton change), revisited with the step-test contract change or when Phase 4's agents need run history, when the fields and the absence of persons are checked against real rows. Decision O3, taken at Phase 3 as recommended in its design (20 November 2026); O3 of 19 November 2026 had left it to this phase.Nothing in Phase 3 needs them, and a reader function is cheap to add later, reviewed against data that exists.
Research Phase 4: the agent harness's design, and the local model on this host (21 November 2026)The owner accepted the Phase 4 design with every recommendation (OD1–OD30): Phase 4 in three parts (4a the machinery with a scripted agent, 4b the local model, 4c the first supervised campaign); a third namespace for the agent machinery, which the notebook hub cannot create pods in, and a second one holding the only key and trace writer; the CPU gate (automatic below 2 CPU-hours, the scientist's approval above, 24 at most per campaign); proposals only, imported from Phase 6. The model layer stays our own gateway with llama.cpp (D4 of 19 November: no vLLM, no LiteLLM). Step 0 measured the local model first: Qwen3-8B generates about 2 tokens a second and Qwen3-4B about 3.8 with a short conversation, and both fall to about 0.25 at 12,288 tokens of context. Decided after it: Qwen3-4B is the provisional model (8B stays downloaded), sessions keep their conversation to about 4,000 tokens (instead of 24,000), and the tool-call eval moves to 4b, where it runs against the real server; the extra measurement of an f32 cache is not made while short conversations suffice. The bench may run beside a recipe run (--during-run, watched by memory and load), its measurements marked.Until the plant model is calibrated, an agent campaign rehearses the machinery rather than giving results to rely on, so the model choice is not worth more hours now. Recorded evidence: research/agents/bench/2026-11-21.json, exercise E51.
The sensors' latency includes the board clock's offset (20 November 2026)The latency of each sensor (0.35 s for the SHT45, 0.66 s for the SCD30 on snapshot 1) is fitted from the time the platform stored a reading minus the time the board stamped it, so it includes any offset between the board's clock and the host's. It is recorded as fitted_confounded and applied as the whole delay; the step-test protocol asks for NTP to be checked on both boards. Implementation choice of 20 November 2026 (design review).The board's clock is set by NTP but not measured; separating the two needs a known event on both clocks, which the lake does not hold.
Fixes from the review of Research Phase 3 (20 November 2026)Five changes to how the calibration reads its data, each tested: (1) the board's cycles, gaps, outages and the publish interval come from the board's own timestamps, and the time the platform received a reading only gives the latency: on snapshot 1 the platform sometimes received a run of cycles late and then all at once, which had been counted as skipped cycles and an outage and pulled the interval to 2.987 s, outside the board's 3.001 s; such delivery stalls are now recorded as not modelled. (2) A noise the fit cannot separate still has an upper bound in the readings; where the model's default is above it, the bound is applied (source upper_bound): the SCD30's CO2 noise is 0.50 ppm instead of the datasheet's 25.6 ppm, which the readings contradict. (3) The plant step fit's interval is widened for the chamber's own wander (a delete-a-block jackknife and the residuals' correlation), so a 2-hour step it accepts is covered and about a third are refused as too uncertain. (4) A calibrated scenario's starting and room humidity, and any change of the room's humidity, are checked against the calibration's range like its setpoints. (5) The fits treat only their own code as making the tree dirty, so the calibration file they write does not block the next fit. The calibration was refitted from the same dataset and the calibrated comparisons run again. Implementation choices of 20 November 2026 (review), recorded for the owner.Each fix makes a recorded number match what the data supports: a calibrated model whose CO2 readings were fifty times noisier than the board's, or an interval that excluded the board's real period, would have been presented as calibrated. Applying the upper bound rather than keeping the default is a choice: the true noise may be smaller still, which the file says. Evidence (20 November 2026). The tests that reproduce each finding fail before and pass after; the refit and the comparisons are recorded under exercise E45's Last done.
Absolute sensor accuracy comes from the datasheet (20 November 2026)No data says how far the reference sensor is from the truth, so the calibration gives each run one constant error per sensor and quantity, drawn from half the datasheet's stated accuracy (standard deviation 0.05 °C and 0.5 %RH for the SHT45; 25.6 ppm CO2 for the SCD30, half of 30 ppm plus 3 % of the 704 ppm it read); the SCD30's temperature and humidity follow the SHT45 through the fitted offsets. The correlation this creates between the two sensors' absolute errors is not modelled and is listed in the calibration file. The draw has its own seeded stream, so a scenario without it gives exactly the readings it gave before. Implementation choice of 20 November 2026 (design review).Dropping absolute error because it cannot be fitted would make the calibrated sensors look more accurate than they are; a datasheet figure, named as such, is the honest default until a reference instrument is used.
Research Phase 4a: the access policy for agent campaigns (21 November 2026)Written, proposed and approved by nobody yet: one skeleton version (the zones research-agents and research-gw, the orchestrator, the session service, the two tool servers and the agent job with their ports, sources and hops, a Keycloak token client research-agent whose tokens carry the audience medcea-research and never medcea-api, the session-token routes and the group research_campaigns in the research zone) and, once it is applied, one change version with the cells decided as OD8: bio_scientist and control_scientist Read, Create and Update, engineer Read, and nothing for qa, auditor or admin. The skeleton version widens only platform-internal reach (no person role gains anything), so any qa person may approve it; the change version gives the three roles above new reach, so those three cannot approve it. Neither version is applied until the owner proposes and a qa person approves it; the platform behaves as before until then.The agent machinery needs its own network zones and a token the platform services refuse, so that a notebook or a compromised pod cannot reach the key holder or the trace writer, and an approver never holds the right they approve.
Research Phase 4b: the local model's pods (skeleton version), proposed, not approved yet (22 November 2026)Written, proposed and approved by nobody yet: one skeleton-only version that adds the pods model-gateway and research-llm to the research gateway zone with their ports, sources and hops, the agent job's hop to the gateway, the gateway among the callers of the session service's server port, and the session-token route POST /v1/turn. No group, no cell and no Keycloak client change, and no person role gains any reach, so any qa person may approve it. Until it is applied the zone's default-deny keeps the two pods apart from everything and a local session cannot start.The model must be reachable only through the gateway, and the gateway only by agent jobs, so that nothing else can ask the model or read its answers; the model itself has no way out of the zone.

Running the platform

This chapter is for the administrator who runs the MedCEA host. It covers installing the platform with ./install.sh, the deploy scripts and the order they run in, the rule that only one deploy runs at a time, and ./medcea.sh, the question-and-answer front end to all of these commands. It then explains the seven IAM switches in config.env that turn the access controls on step by step (and WORKBENCH_ENABLED, which medcea.sh switches the same way), which of them a fresh install leaves off and how to turn those on, what the health check reports, which IAM test scripts to run and what a good result looks like, how operators are given units, how to uninstall, how the domain names reach other devices through Tailscale, and the credentials file. It ends with troubleshooting for problems an administrator can meet. Run every command from the repository root on the host.

Installing and updating

./install.sh is the one entry point. It runs three stages in order: the infrastructure (./deploy-infra.sh), every application (./deploy-apps.sh --all), and the health check (./health-check.sh). While IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true (a new config.env's default since 8 November 2026) it runs the infrastructure once more between the applications and the health check, and says why ("IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true: the infrastructure runs once more, so Grafana and pgAdmin move onto their own database roles (svc_grafana, rr_admin_login) now that the database lets them log in."): Grafana and pgAdmin are deployed by the first stage, before the database deploy in the applications stage lets their roles log in. It is the switch's own enable recipe, under the same deploy lock; a failure stops the install like any stage. The same command updates an existing install: finished steps are skipped or updated in place, so it is safe to run again after a pull or after a failure. If a stage fails, the script stops, names the stage and its log file in logs/, and tells you to fix the cause and run it again.

CommandWhat it does
./install.shInstall or update everything: infrastructure, applications, the infrastructure again while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true, health check. Asks for any missing settings first.
./install.sh --configureReview every setting (current values offered as defaults), then install.
./install.sh --infra-onlyOnly the infrastructure: MicroK8s, PostgreSQL, Keycloak, Grafana, Node-RED, the portal and the AI workbench.
./install.sh --apps-onlyOnly the applications. Needs the infrastructure and config.env. While IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is true it ends with "Still to do, unless ./deploy-infra.sh has run since this database deploy: ./deploy-infra.sh, so Grafana and pgAdmin move onto their own database roles".
./install.sh --helpThe options, including the uninstall levels (see Uninstalling).

At the end of an install the script prints, in this order: "MedCEA is installed" with the portal's address, or, when the infrastructure stage listed a problem it went on past (the platform's names do not resolve on this machine, the name server does not answer, the AI workbench failed) or the health check found a failure, "Finished with problems" and one "Still to do" line for each; while any IAM switch is still false, one line pointing to ./medcea.sh → IAM switches → Bring IAM to full enforcement (see After a fresh install; a fresh install always prints it); when the applications stage skipped Superset, a "Still to do" line saying why and what to run (see Superset); then the steps for trusting the platform's certificate authority on your devices, and the credentials box last, so it stays on screen (see The credentials file).

config.env and the setup questions

All settings live in config.env in the repository root. It is not in git and is readable only by its owner (mode 600), because it holds every platform password. You do not write it by hand: the first run of ./deploy-infra.sh (or ./install.sh) creates it from config.env.example by asking questions. Press Enter to accept the value shown in brackets. Later runs ask only for required values that are still empty. To review every setting, run ./deploy-infra.sh --configure, or ./infra/configure.sh to edit the settings without deploying.

The questions cover:

  • Project name (PROJECT_NAME, default medcea): the MQTT topic root, the Kubernetes namespace and the Keycloak realm. Lowercase, starting with a letter, 2 to 31 characters from a-z 0-9 -. Changing it after boards are flashed means reflashing them.
  • Domain (DOMAIN): every web page is served at <service>.<DOMAIN>. The menu offers a name (for example medcea, so the portal is portal.medcea) when Tailscale is up, the Tailscale or LAN IP with nip.io, or a custom domain of your own. For a custom domain it then asks who answers DNS for it: this platform, on this server (the default: Tailscale split DNS or your LAN router sends lookups for the domain here, or nothing is set up yet), which sets LOCAL_DNS="true"; or a DNS server elsewhere that already has an A record for every <service>.<domain>, which sets it to false. When Tailscale split DNS already sends the domain to this server, it does not ask: the platform must answer there. With Tailscale up it also asks which address other devices use, the Tailscale one or the LAN one; that answer sets USE_TAILSCALE and which address PLATFORM_IP takes (see A domain of your own). Changing the domain later means running ./deploy-infra.sh again.
  • The platform administrator: username, a real e-mail address you read (Keycloak password resets go there, and it is the pgAdmin login) and password. Addresses on special-use domains (.local, .test, .invalid, .example, .localhost, .arpa, .onion) are refused here and for the qa person and the engineer: pgAdmin will not start with one.
  • The first qa person and the first engineer: username and e-mail for each. The qa person must be someone other than the administrator. Their initial passwords are generated and replaced at their first sign-in.
  • The PostgreSQL superuser password, the database volume size, and your Docker Hub username and access token (needed to pull the Bitnami Helm charts).
  • On the first run (no config.env yet) and on a full review (--configure): the time zone for Node-RED flows and schedules; the backup folder (BACKUP_DIR, an absolute path, default /var/backups/<project>; better on another disk than the data's, and when you cannot write its parent the applications stage asks for sudo once to create it) and the days to keep backups (BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS); and whether to deploy the AI workbench.

Some values are generated and never asked: the qa and engineer initial passwords, the Keycloak break-glass console account (kc-breakglass) and its password, and the passwords of the database service roles. Configuration also checks for Tailscale on every run. USE_TAILSCALE records whether the domain depends on it: when it is true, a deploy stops if Tailscale is down, rather than quietly falling back to the LAN address.

Password rules

A password you type must be 8 to 64 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ ~ - only. Other punctuation breaks the URLs and YAML files the password is written into, so the question asks again. Password input is hidden and typed twice. Pressing Enter generates a 20-character password (or keeps the current one if there is one), shows it once, and lists it in the credentials file.

Every command writes its own log in logs/ (readable by the platform user only): deploy-infra-<timestamp>.log, deploy-apps-…, a component deployed on its own app-<component>-deploy-… (or -uninstall-…), app-iam-units-…, deploy-workbench-…, health-check-…, the throwaway database test iam-db-fixture-<command>-… and each live test iam-<name>-…. A command run by another (a component by ./deploy-apps.sh, a test by the fixture) writes into its caller's log. The first line of the output names the file. MEDCEA_NO_LOG=1 turns it off for one run.

Configuration runs before the deploy log starts, so your answers and generated passwords never reach logs/. Its host package check is the exception: when a package is missing, what it reports, its question and apt-get's output go to logs/prereqs-<timestamp>.log (your answer and the sudo password do not), so a deploy stopped there still leaves a record. When configuration rebuilds config.env on a newer config.env.example (keeping your values), it saves the previous file as config.env.bak.

The deploy scripts and their order

install.sh is a thin wrapper. Each stage also works on its own, and after the first install you will usually run the stages directly.

ScriptWhat it deploys
./deploy-infra.shMicroK8s (bootstrapped only on the first run), PostgreSQL, Keycloak with the realm, clients and roles, the MQTT broker, Node-RED, Grafana, pgAdmin, the sign-in proxies, the portal, the AI workbench (unless WORKBENCH_ENABLED=false), the access policy's route table and the realm's public keys. It writes a log to logs/deploy-infra-<timestamp>.log.
./deploy-apps.shA checkbox menu of the application components under apps/. ./deploy-apps.sh --all deploys every component without asking.
./apps/<component>/deploy.shOne component on its own. The components are access, backup (the nightly backup, see Backup and restore), database, edge-wizard, frontend, iam, monitor, mqtt-explorer, node-red, report, scheduler and superset (skipped while the applied access policy gives no role a Superset setting, while IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is not true, and while no version of the policy is applied, see Superset) (./deploy-apps.sh --help lists them).
./infra/deploy-workbench.shRedeploys only the AI workbench (JupyterHub, chart 4.4.4: JupyterHub 5.5.4). A workspace that is already running keeps its old setup until it is stopped and started again. Who may sign in and who is hub administrator come from the access policy; if the policy does not compile, the script stops before it changes anything and the running workbench stays as it is.

The order rules are:

  • Infrastructure first. The applications need the cluster, Keycloak and PostgreSQL that deploy-infra.sh creates. ./install.sh --apps-only refuses without config.env.
  • Database before scheduler. deploy-apps.sh runs components in alphabetical order, so database comes before scheduler. When you deploy them one by one, run ./apps/database/deploy.sh first: the scheduler deploy refuses until the database functions it needs exist.
  • Access after infrastructure. Run ./deploy-infra.sh, then ./apps/access/deploy.sh. The access deploy runs the database deploy itself when it needs to. Since 1 November 2026 the order also matters for Sign out: ./deploy-infra.sh registers the AI Workbench's logout address with each app's sign-in, and the access deploy then points Sign out at it. In the other order, Sign out shows Keycloak's "Invalid redirect uri" and ends nothing until ./deploy-infra.sh has run.
  • After a pull of new IAM code: ./deploy-infra.sh (the route table), then ./apps/database/deploy.sh, then ./deploy-apps.sh --all while no recipe run is active. Until all three have run, the health check's iamgrants and tests/iam-schema.sh stay red.
  • From IAM 4.2a, every deploy that compiles the access policy reads the applied version from PostgreSQL first and refuses while PostgreSQL is not Ready; ./deploy-infra.sh repairs PostgreSQL before it reads the policy, so run it first in that case. A git change that gives access is refused by every deploy (see The skeleton gate).
  • iam-api (the iam component, IAM 3.5) after ./apps/database/deploy.sh and ./apps/access/deploy.sh: alphabetical order already does this. While IAM_DB_SERVICE_ROLES is false (an older config.env) it is skipped with a warning. A new config.env has it true, so a fresh install deploys iam-api and the Access Policy; there, confirming and approving answer "need IAM_POSTGREST_JWT=true and IAM_DB_ROLES=true" until both switches are on. Then turn on IAM_MQTT_PERSON (see IAM switches).
  • After rotating or removing a realm key in Keycloak, run ./deploy-infra.sh. It republishes the keys and restarts config-api when they changed.
  • pgAdmin restarts whenever ./deploy-infra.sh changes its sign-in settings (pgAdmin's client secret, the roles it admits, or ADMIN_PASS), which signs everyone out of pgAdmin; a run that changes none of them leaves it running. Only on an install deployed before 1 November 2026 (not after a fresh install, where the secret never left the Kubernetes Secret): the first ./deploy-infra.sh after that date restarts pgAdmin once, when its secrets move into a Kubernetes Secret, and removes the older copies of pgAdmin's deployment that still held them; pgAdmin's client secret was readable in plain text until then, so give it a new one once: in the Keycloak console, realm medcea, Clients, pgadmin, Credentials, Regenerate; then run ./deploy-infra.sh, which reads the new secret and restarts pgAdmin.
  • pgAdmin's IoT Postgres entry is loaded for each account that may sign in to pgAdmin when pgAdmin starts. ./deploy-infra.sh lists the e-mail addresses of the enabled Keycloak accounts holding a role pgAdmin admits (admin) and gives the list to pgAdmin; when the list changed, pgAdmin restarts (everyone is signed out of it) and loads the entry for each address, which can add several minutes to its start. So after giving someone the admin role, or changing an admin's e-mail address, run ./deploy-infra.sh: until then they can sign in to pgAdmin but see no server. An account without an e-mail address, or with one on a reserved test domain such as .invalid, .test or .example (pgAdmin refuses those), gets no entry; the deploy names it in a warning. If Keycloak cannot be read, the deploy keeps the list pgAdmin already has, so nobody loses their entry, and says so; only when pgAdmin has no list yet does it go on with the platform administrator's address alone. Since 1 November 2026 pgAdmin runs version 9.19.0, pinned in k8s/pgadmin/pgadmin.yaml; on an install from before that date the first ./deploy-infra.sh after it restarts pgAdmin once.
  • Node-RED after ./deploy-infra.sh: when Node-RED's settings changed, the deploy restarts it. Its flows are kept on a volume and survive. The first deploy onto that volume (and a fresh install) starts with no flows; the deploy then says "Node-RED runs no flows" and telemetry is not stored until you run ./apps/node-red/deploy.sh. Do that first deploy while no recipe run is active.

The scheduler runs recipe code straight from the repository (schd/), and the onboarding wizard runs edge/ from it. Do not pull or edit the repository while a recipe run is active: check first that pgrep -af '[r]un_recipe.py' prints nothing.

When your login session is not yet in the microk8s group (for example right after the first install added you to it), the scripts run their microk8s calls through sudo and say why they ask for your password. Log out and back in to stop that.

IAM 4.1: deploying the policy versions schema

Slice 4.1 adds the database side of policy versions (migration 008c), a function the access component installs (iam._changed_since) and every Phase 4 entry of the access policy. Nothing calls them yet. After pulling it, run three deploys in this order, back to back, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.1, which holds the deploy lock for all three:

  1. ./apps/access/deploy.sh. It must come first: the database deploy refuses without iam._changed_since ("run ./apps/access/deploy.sh first (IAM 4.1)"), and the health check's iamgrants is red from the pull until this step.
  2. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: migration 008c, the compiled functions and the grants.
  3. ./deploy-infra.sh, at once: the new route table, which the User Manager reads within a minute, and the NetworkPolicies.

From the end of step 2 until the User Manager has read the route table of step 3 (about one to two minutes), the User Manager answers 503 to a grant, an activation, or a role change into qa, qp, admin or auditor: the database and the route table disagree about what such a change widens (the new policy_page row). Do not grant or change roles until all three deploys have finished. A refused decision changed nothing and can simply be repeated. Every other decision and every other service is unaffected.

Between steps 2 and 3 the health check's iamgrants and tests/iam-schema.sh are red; after step 3 and one minute, everything is green. To take slice 4.1 back out, while no policy version exists: run apps/database/medcea_db_migrations_down_008c.sql as postgres in one transaction (the command is in its header), then revert the code, then ./apps/database/deploy.sh and ./deploy-infra.sh; the 503 window opens in reverse. The down file refuses once a version exists.

IAM 4.2a: version 1 and the skeleton gate

Slice 4.2a turns the access policy into numbered versions on this host. The database records version 1 (the factory policy of apps/iam/policy/defaults.yaml, applied at once), every deploy then compiles from the applied version (the host file state/policy-applied.yaml, see Policy source), and every deploy runs the skeleton gate. Nobody's access changes: version 1 compiles to exactly what defaults.yaml compiled to before. After pulling it, check that git status -- apps/iam shows nothing (the bootstrap refuses uncommitted changes there), then run three deploys in this order, back to back, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.2a, which asks your username (--by) and holds the deploy lock for all three:

  1. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: the 4.2a database functions (the policy's system actors, the event rules, the filter of the policy history) and the grants. It must come first: the other two record events through these functions.
  2. ./deploy-infra.sh, at once: the route table's digest moves once (it no longer counts the name of the policy file), and the accounts the install seeded are recorded in the policy history (account_seeded, see the policy history).
  3. MEDCEA_POLICY_BOOTSTRAP_BY=<your username> ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: no policy version exists yet, so it runs ./apps/iam/apply.sh --bootstrap --by <you> (without the variable, the platform administrator ADMIN_USER is named). It checks every compile is unchanged, writes version 1 in one database transaction, writes state/policy-applied.yaml, checks the grants, records bootstrap_applied, and restarts iam-api as every iam deploy does.

There is no 503 window: no grant or role changes. Between steps 1 and 2 the health check's iamenforce and tests/iam-schema.sh are red for a few minutes, because the database and the route table disagree about the digest; after step 2 they are green. Step 3 prints [iam] Policy versions..., then the bootstrap's lines (state empty, the tree's commit, the account you named, "version 1 compiles to exactly what defaults.yaml compiles to (N targets): nothing is re-rendered", [policy] state/policy-applied.yaml: version 1 (bootstrap) written, the grants check, the report) and ends "version 1 (bootstrap) applied: nothing was re-rendered". The health check then has two more checks, 54 in all (55 since the Platform manual check of 3 November 2026, 56 since the Superset roles check of 6 November 2026): Access policy version (OK: "version 1 (bootstrap), qa confirms it in the Policy UI once it exists (IAM 4.3)") and Policy artefacts (OK; the Policy UI's host is counted as not deployed). Then run tests/iam-schema.sh and ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status.

If the bootstrap waits (Keycloak not reachable, or a --by that is not an enabled account with a person_id), the iam deploy warns and finishes, and Access policy version FAILs "no applied version: a widening git change is not gated until version 1 exists" until ./apps/iam/deploy.sh runs again. On a fresh install the same happens inside ./install.sh: the iam component bootstraps version 1 in ./deploy-apps.sh --all.

Taking slice 4.2a back out. Version 1 and its events stay in the database, frozen; the down file of 008c refuses while they exist, by design. Under the deploy lock, while the 4.2a code is still there, move the host's policy files aside: bash -c 'source infra/lib-lock.sh && medcea_lock && source infra/lib-policy-source.sh && policy_state_retire rollback' (it moves state/policy-applied.yaml, state/seed-facts.jsonl, state/break-glass/ and the mark state/.policy-versioned into state/retired-<time>-rollback/; the 4.1 code refuses a host file). Then revert the slice in git, run ./apps/database/deploy.sh (the 4.1 functions come back) and ./deploy-infra.sh (the route table's digest moves back once). Applying 4.2a again later finds version 1 and does not bootstrap again.

The applied access policy

From slice 4.2a the access policy in force is the database's applied version, not the file in git. apps/iam/policy/defaults.yaml stays the factory file: version 1 was made from it, and it still holds the platform's skeleton (roles, resource groups and their routes, hosts, the network rules, the invariants: everything but the matrix of who holds which level, and the waivers). The matrix and the waivers come from the applied version.

IAM 4.3: the Policy UI

Slice 4.3 (November 2026) adds the Access Policy at https://policy.<domain>: iam-api serves it on a second port (8083, Service iam-admin) behind its own sign-in proxy (iam-oauth2-proxy, Keycloak client policy). Nobody's access changes and the policy is not changed. Run three deploys in this order, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.3 (the Policy UI), which holds the deploy lock for all three:

  1. ./deploy-infra.sh: the Keycloak client policy (with groups, person_id and the medcea-api audience), policy.<domain> in the certificate and the name service, the portal's Access Policy card, and POLICY_DOMAIN, POLICY_CLIENT_SECRET and POLICY_COOKIE_SECRET in config.env.
  2. ./apps/access/deploy.sh: the User Manager's Access Policy link, and Sign out on the new address.
  3. ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: ConfigMap iam-compiler (the policy compiler and the factory file, about 360 KiB, applied server-side), iam-api with its second port, then the sign-in proxy. Like the User Manager's, the proxy admits admin only until every iam-api pod answers on port 8083 that it enforces, then admin, auditor, qa and qp; without that answer the deploy stops with "the Policy UI's gate stays admin-only".

Afterwards the health check has one warning on purpose: Access policy version "version 1 (bootstrap) is not confirmed by qa yet (the Policy UI)", until a qa person confirms it (exercise E16). From then on the check also fails when the Policy UI shows another applied version than the database, and warns when it ships another skeleton than the accepted one (run ./apps/iam/deploy.sh). ./apps/iam/deploy.sh --gate-only re-renders the Policy UI's proxy when it drifted. To remove it: ./apps/iam/uninstall.sh (the proxy, the second port, the compiler ConfigMap and the card); the Keycloak client stays, and a confirmation already recorded stays in the history.

IAM 4.4: drafting and approval

Slice 4.4 (November 2026) lets an admin draft a change to the access policy in the Access Policy and a qa person approve it there, and lets the host operator propose a git skeleton change for the same approval (apply.sh --propose-skeleton, below). Nothing approved is applied in 4.4: applying a version came with slice 4.5 (below). Nobody's access changes, no grant changes and there is no 503 window. Run two deploys in this order, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.4 (drafting and approval), which holds the deploy lock for both:

  1. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: the new bodies of the policy's approve and why-not functions (break-glass blocks approvals; a skeleton version needs the attestation, a fresh proposal and an approver whose role it does not widen). No new table, column, function or grant.
  2. ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: iam-api with the write side of the Policy UI, the new page, and ConfigMap iam-compiler with the new diff code (its checksum restarts iam-api).

In the minute between the two the old page still serves and cannot write: harmless. ./deploy-infra.sh and the access deploy are not needed (the route table, the proxies and the clients do not change). Approving needs IAM_POSTGREST_JWT and IAM_DB_ROLES to be true, as confirming does. The health check stays green after the deploy. It WARNs "version N (<kind>) is approved: ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> applies it" (since slice 4.5; until then "applying it arrives with IAM 4.5") for as long as an approved version waits, "skeleton version N was proposed against skeleton …, the accepted one is now …: return it and propose again" when a deploy accepted a narrowing under a proposal, and, as before, an open version older than 7 days.

Taking slice 4.4 back out.

  1. ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status must show no open change or skeleton version. If one is open, withdraw it: in the Policy UI (an admin, while the 4.4 page still serves), or from the host with ./apps/iam/apply.sh --withdraw-open --by <you> --reason "<why>" (when the page is the reason for the rollback, or after the revert: the 4.3 page has no Withdraw). Last resort, with the 4.4 apply.sh already reverted: SELECT iam_policy._withdraw_open('<reason>') as postgres in the PostgreSQL pod (actor system:apply). An approved 4.4 version must not survive a revert of 4.4: it was approved under 4.4's checks, which the reverted code no longer makes, and slice 4.5 could otherwise apply it.
  2. Revert the slice in git.
  3. The same two deploys.

What stays, by design: the withdrawn and approved versions, their events and their evidence (permanent); a proposed skeleton that was never accepted (harmless). The reverted approve function no longer refuses under break-glass and no longer checks skeleton versions.

IAM 4.5: applying versions

Slice 4.5 (November 2026) applies what a qa person approved: ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> for a change or skeleton version, ./apps/iam/apply.sh --rollback-to K --by <you> --reason "<why>" to restore an earlier version, and ./apps/iam/apply.sh --audit N to check an applied version afterwards (apply.sh). The deploy itself changes nobody's access, no grant and no gate, and has no 503 window. Run four deploys in this order, best through ./medcea.sh → Policy → Deploy IAM 4.5 (applying versions), which holds the deploy lock for all of them:

  1. ./apps/database/deploy.sh: new_draft refuses a draft while the applied version's last apply event is unfinished (apply_started or partial_apply), whatever events were filed after it.
  2. ./apps/access/deploy.sh: the User Manager reads who approves and who makes account changes from the route table's dual_control, not from a list in its code (proof-gated as before; no access change).
  3. ./apps/iam/deploy.sh: the Access Policy shows the apply states ("applied — rollout incomplete", "approved — a previous apply was reverted") and a rollback's Confirm card; ConfigMap iam-compiler carries the new compiler code, so iam-api restarts.
  4. ./apps/backup/deploy.sh: the nightly backup's MANIFEST names the policy history's head (its id and hash) at the time of the dump.

apply.sh, its checks and health-check.sh run on the host and need no deploy. After the deploy the health check stays green; it WARNs "version N (<kind>) is approved: ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> applies it" while an approved version waits.

Taking slice 4.5 back out. First ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status: no version may be left apply_started or partial_apply (any outcome: run --resume first), and no open change or skeleton version (withdraw it). Then revert the slice in git and run the same four deploys. The versions applied by 4.5 stay applied and keep their events; the 4.4 code reads them as it reads version 1.

Policy source

Every compile of the policy (every deploy, the health check, the onboarding wizard, flash-device.sh) reads the host file state/policy-applied.yaml when it exists. It is the applied version composed with the accepted skeleton, written by the deploy scripts under the deploy lock: by ./apps/iam/apply.sh after it applies a version, and by every deploy that finds it missing or different from the database. Nobody edits it by hand. state/ is readable by the deploying account only (mode 700, the file 600) and is not in git. Its first two lines say what it is:

# medcea-applied: version=1 kind=bootstrap entries_digest=… skeleton_digest=… git_commit=… written_at=…
# medcea-applied-body: body_digest=… groups=… roles=… dropped=0 keys=…

Every compile checks those lines against the body: a file edited by hand or cut short stops every deploy and the onboarding wizard with "its header does not match its body (edited by hand, or truncated)". Restore it with ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you> if an apply was interrupted, or with any deploy, which rewrites it from the database. Health compares the whole body with the database's rows as well (Access policy version).

Before compiling, each deploy reads the applied version from PostgreSQL:

  • No version yet (before the bootstrap, or before migration 008c): the deploy compiles defaults.yaml. A host file at that point is refused: "state/policy-applied.yaml names a version but the database has no policy versions".
  • PostgreSQL not Ready: the deploy refuses and compiles nothing, with or without a host file. ./deploy-infra.sh is the one that repairs PostgreSQL: right after the Kubernetes API answers it only checks the skeleton gate (when the database can be asked; a widening git change stops it there, before anything changes), and it reads the applied policy only after its PostgreSQL step, so run it first. ./deploy-apps.sh asks PostgreSQL once before its first component that compiles the policy and stops the whole run when it is not Ready.
  • A host file without its database (after a restore of an older dump, or a database dropped by hand): restore the database the file belongs to, or move the file aside with policy_state_retire as in Restoring step 2a, only after reading this section. The next deploy then writes it again from the database. apps/database/uninstall.sh --purge-data (after its DROP), ./deploy-infra.sh --reset (after the namespace is gone) and --uninstall (after MicroK8s is removed) do this themselves, under the deploy lock, into state/retired-<time>-<why>/; nothing is deleted.
  • A version was applied here, but the host file is missing: the first host file also writes the mark state/.policy-versioned. While it exists, a compile outside a deploy (the onboarding wizard at its start, flash-device.sh) refuses "state/policy-applied.yaml is absent, but a policy version was applied on this host" instead of falling back to defaults.yaml, which may hold an unreviewed change. The next deploy writes the file again. A restore's step 2a keeps the mark; a deploy that then finds a database with no applied version (a dump older than the bootstrap) moves the mark into state/retired-<time>-no-version/ itself. A purge, a reset and an uninstall move it with the rest.
  • Versions exist but none is applied: refused; see ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status.

What these checks defend against, and what they do not. They stop a widening of access from reaching a deploy through the platform's own tools: a change in git, a variable left exported in a shell, a file edited during a deploy, a stale or hand-edited state/ file, a cold or crashed PostgreSQL, a restore or a purge. They do not stop the account that deploys the platform from going round them on purpose (it can run psql as postgres, edit the scripts, or rewrite the host file with recomputed digests): that is the host operator's break-glass, found afterwards through the policy history, the version audit and the health check, not prevented. A host file forged that way passes the compile's own checks, is found by the health check, and is overwritten by the next deploy; the onboarding wizard can compile it in between (see known gaps).

Two edge cases: flash-device.sh run from another clone of the repository, which has no state/, compiles defaults.yaml (harmless while version 1 equals it; it matters once a later version differs, IAM 4.5). The onboarding wizard compiles once when it starts, so a new applied version reaches it only at its next restart (./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh --gate-only restarts it only when its roles changed).

The skeleton gate

Every deploy compares the skeleton in git with the skeleton the platform accepted last. A change that gives access is refused before anything is compiled or changed. It counts as giving access when it adds, for any role: a route, a host, a database privilege or row filter, a tool setting, an MQTT topic or a level; and also, for nobody in particular: a route anyone may call without signing in, an upstream every signed-in host reaches, a host's service or client, a network source allowed into a pod, a host outside the sign-in proxies, a hop or a token client of a calling pod, any privilege or membership of a service identity, any database row filter, and any weakening of the checker's own rules (the invariants, the waivable list, break-glass, the database roles, the levels, the resource types, the classes, the constraints, the schema version). Help texts and descriptions do not count. The deploy stops with:

ERROR: this git change gives access that has not been approved (skeleton <git> over the accepted <accepted>):
  <role>: <n> new: route iam GET /api/… ; …
  anonymous and services: public monitor GET /api/… ; …
This change needs a qa-approved skeleton version: put HEAD back at the accepted skeleton, keep the change as a commit on a branch, and run ./apps/iam/apply.sh --propose-skeleton --by <you> --reason "<why>" --from-git <commit>; once qa approves it, check that commit out and run ./apps/iam/apply.sh <version>.
Break-glass (MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE) does not bypass this check: it changes the matrix, never the skeleton.
Nothing was changed.

The network rules count in full: besides each pod's allowed sources, any change to how a source is resolved (the ingress namespace, a proxy's release name, a pod's or a calling pod's selector, the ports a pod carries, a calling pod's only_rpc list, the hosts that skip the shared upstreams) is a change that gives access, and so is any change to a database role name, a service identity's MQTT login or database password variable, or the MQTT Explorer's credential settings. Removing an allowed source, a rule, a hop, a resource group or a role only narrows. A key the gate does not know yet counts as giving access too (developers classify it in apps/iam/compiler/explain.py; tests/test_policy_source.py fails until they do). The refusal names such a change "section <key> changed".

The way forward for such a change: put HEAD back at the accepted skeleton, keep the change as a commit on a branch, and propose that commit as a skeleton version (./apps/iam/apply.sh --propose-skeleton --by <you> --reason "<why>" --from-git <commit>, since slice 4.4); a qa person approves it in the Access Policy. While the proposal waits, the deploying tree stays at the accepted skeleton; a tree that carries it is refused by every deploy, and the health check FAILs "the git skeleton widens: a deploy refuses it (proposed as version N, <status>: put HEAD back at the accepted skeleton; the proposal waits on its branch)". Once it is approved, check its commit out and run ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> (since slice 4.5): the gate lets through exactly the approved skeleton, and only when HEAD contains the proposal's commit; the refusal then reads "This skeleton is approved as version N: run ./apps/iam/apply.sh N --by <you> to apply it (deploys refuse it until then)".

Keep the skeleton commit on the deployed branch. Once skeleton version N is applied, the accepted skeleton is that commit's. A checkout that drops it (an older branch, a reset) is a narrowing to the next deploy, which accepts it without asking: the approved access is silently gone. To undo an applied skeleton version on purpose, git revert the skeleton change and deploy (the deploy accepts the narrowing and records it), plus --rollback-to for the matrix if needed. A skeleton version is never reverted automatically.

A change that only narrows access, or changes nothing a person can reach, is checked first: the git skeleton with the applied matrix must pass the policy checker, otherwise the deploy refuses "the git skeleton … with the applied matrix fails the checker; it is not accepted and nothing was changed" (fix the change in git). When it passes, it is accepted by the next deploy and recorded (skeleton_accepted, with the skeleton it replaced, and skeleton_synced); the health check WARNs "the git skeleton narrows: accepted at the next deploy" until then. A change to the matrix: in git is not refused but has no effect: the matrix comes from the applied version (the health check WARNs "git may lag"). ./apps/iam/apply.sh --status shows the accepted and the git skeleton; developers check a change offline with python3 apps/iam/compiler/cli.py skeleton-gate --against-git HEAD --check.

Policy break-glass

When a deploy must compile another matrix than the applied version's (an emergency, before approvals exist), break-glass names a policy file of your own for one run: MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE=<file> MEDCEA_POLICY_BREAK_GLASS="<reason>" ./apps/<component>/deploy.sh (or ./deploy-infra.sh). Without the reason the deploy refuses ("set MEDCEA_POLICY_BREAK_GLASS=<reason>"). For several components at once, export MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE and run ./deploy-apps.sh [--all] --break-glass "<reason>" (asked once, one event naming every selected component that compiles the policy) or ./install.sh --break-glass "<reason>" (asked once, two events: the infrastructure and the applications). Without --break-glass, deploy-apps.sh and install.sh ignore an exported MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE and say so. ./medcea.sh → Policy → How to use policy break-glass shows the same and runs nothing.

  • Break-glass does not bypass the skeleton gate. A git change that gives access is refused under break-glass too, before anything is recorded.
  • It changes only the matrix and the waivers. The file's skeleton must equal the accepted one, and its rows for iam_policy and iam_users must equal the applied version's: break-glass can never change who approves policy or account changes.
  • The deploy prints the file and the reason and asks you to type the word break-glass at the terminal (deploy-apps.sh/install.sh --break-glass ask once for the whole run); without a terminal it refuses.
  • The file is copied to state/break-glass/<time>-<pid>.yaml; that copy is what is compiled, so editing the original afterwards changes nothing. The copy stays as evidence.
  • Before any compile, the deploy records break_glass_seen in the policy history (the copy's SHA-256, the reason, your OS account, the component) and prints in red "BREAK-GLASS: compiling … recorded as event N".
  • The health check's Access policy version FAILs while it is open. It ends per component: that component's next successful deploy without MEDCEA_POLICY_FILE records break_glass_ended as its last step (a deploy that fails leaves it open). ./deploy-infra.sh (infrastructure and, when enabled, the AI workbench) and ./deploy-apps.sh --all end it everywhere. The onboarding wizard's component ends only on a machine with a user session (its deploy skips otherwise).
  • Write the reason and the decision in your operations log.

Re-rendering only what drifted

Since slice 4.2b (November 2026) each script that deploys something compiled from the access policy has a scoped mode. It compiles its targets, compares each with what the cluster runs, prints one line per target (unchanged, re-rendered, not deployed or deferred) and changes only what differs. A second run therefore prints unchanged everywhere and changes nothing. Use it when the health check's Policy artefacts names a stale target, or after the host file changed; ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume runs all of them for you. ./medcea.sh → Policy → Re-render the policy artefacts runs them in one lock.

CommandTargetsOn a drift
./deploy-infra.sh --policy-onlyThe route table and MQTT rows (ConfigMap medcea-iam-lib), the application pods' network policies, Node-RED's editor rights, Grafana's roles, pgAdmin's sign-in roles, the Node-RED and portal gatesRe-renders that target only. iam-api restarts only when the MQTT rows changed, and the MQTT Explorer credentials issued under the old rows end, as in a full deploy. Grafana and pgAdmin redeploy their whole section (they restart; pgAdmin's sessions end), and only for pgAdmin is Keycloak asked who gets the database entry. Logs to logs/deploy-infra-policy-<time>.log.
./infra/deploy-workbench.sh --policy-onlyThe AI workbench's gate (who may sign in, hub administrators, the refusal message) and the notebooks' network hopsThe same Helm upgrade as a full deploy; the hub restarts only because its values changed. The example notebooks are not touched. In the research zone (research Phase 2b) it also compares the hook that gives the hub administrator no workspace. While the workbench runs in the namespace the policy no longer names it prints deferred and exits 4: run ./infra/deploy-workbench.sh --move, then ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you> (Moving the AI workbench).
./apps/<c>/deploy.sh --gate-only for frontend, scheduler, monitor, mqtt-explorer, accessThe sign-in gate of that application's host(s): the roles it admits and its 403 pageA Helm upgrade of that proxy only; it rolls by itself because its configuration changed. No other part of the application is touched and nothing is restarted. The User Manager's gate widens only after every access pod proves it enforces, as in a full deploy; without the proof it stays admin-only and the command fails.
./apps/iam/deploy.sh --gate-onlyThe Policy UI's gate (since slice 4.3)A Helm upgrade of iam-oauth2-proxy, proof-gated like the User Manager's.
./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh --gate-onlyThe roles the onboarding wizard admits (its --required-role)Restarts the wizard service, which compiles them when it starts. While an onboarding run is in progress it does not restart (that would kill the run): it prints deferred and exits 4. Run ./apps/iam/apply.sh --resume --by <you> after the run has finished.
./apps/superset/deploy.sh --gate-onlySuperset's role mapping (since Superset stage C)Rewrites Secret superset-secrets and ConfigMap superset-config and restarts Superset, which installs its packages from the wheel cache; it also counts a pod started with an older Secret as drift. Stops Superset when the policy no longer gives a role a setting. While the wheel cache is incomplete it prints deferred and exits 4 if the running Superset admits only what the policy still gives, and stops it otherwise (see Superset).

None of these touches Keycloak's realm, the database (except ending outdated MQTT credentials, as above), the TLS certificates or DNS, and none restarts an application, except two gates that are read only at start: the onboarding wizard's (./apps/edge-wizard/deploy.sh --gate-only restarts the cea-edge-wizard service on drift) and Superset's (its --gate-only restarts Superset). The database grants have no scoped mode: ./apps/database/deploy.sh applies them.

The deploy scripts refuse an option they do not know (exit 2, nothing runs). Before 4.2b a mistyped option such as ./deploy-infra.sh --polcy-only ran a full deploy.

apply.sh

./apps/iam/apply.sh applies policy versions. As of slice 4.5 it has these modes; it logs to logs/apply-policy-<time>.log:

CommandWhat it doesLock
--bootstrap --by <username>Version 1 from the factory file, only while no version exists. The iam deploy runs it; by hand only when that waited. Asks you to type yes (a permanent record).yes
--bootstrap --check-only --by <username>Would version 1 bootstrap? Writes nothing.no
--resume --by <username>Finishes an apply that was committed but did not record its end, or one with a deferred target: rewrites the host file, runs every scoped mode under its lock (each re-renders only what drifted), checks the grants, records the end. A target that had to wait (the onboarding wizard during an onboarding run) is recorded as apply_deferred after the end; the health check's Access policy version WARNs until a later --resume re-renders it. The iam deploy runs --resume itself when it finds an unfinished apply. Asks [y/N].yes
--statusThe applied version (who it is claimed by, whether qa confirmed it), open versions, the last policy events, the accepted and git skeleton, the host file, the live digests, open break-glass, recorded and queued account facts.no
--propose-skeleton --by <username> --reason "<text>" --from-git <rev> [--check-only]Since slice 4.4. Proposes the skeleton of commit <rev> (--from-git is mandatory: the deploying tree stays at the accepted skeleton) as a submitted version of kind skeleton, for a qa person's approval in the Access Policy. Only a skeleton that widens access and passes the checker with the applied matrix is proposed ("nothing to approve" otherwise), never under break-glass, never while another change or skeleton version is open. --by is resolved in Keycloak and recorded as the proposer (a claim); the --by username and your OS user are appended to the reason. It prints what each role gains, the digests, and which roles a qa approver may not approve for; asks [y/N]; writes the version and its diff in one transaction (system:apply). Nothing is applied. --check-only writes nothing and takes no lock.yes
--withdraw-open --by <username> --reason "<text>" [--check-only]Since slice 4.4. Withdraws the one open change or skeleton version (draft, submitted or approved) from the host, when the Access Policy cannot (a rollback of 4.4, an aborted test). Shows the version and its authors and asks [y/N]; "nothing is open" exits 0. --by is not looked up in Keycloak (withdrawing grants nothing); it and your OS user are appended to the reason. The withdrawn event names system:apply.yes
<N> --by <username> [--check-only]Since slice 4.5. Applies change or skeleton version N, approved by a qa person in the Access Policy, from a committed tree (uncommitted changes in apps/iam are refused). Before anything changes it checks, and refuses with the reason: the version is approved and based on the applied one, the last apply finished, no open break-glass, the history chain; the approval's token is a realm signature with the expected claims (verified against the key Keycloak publishes now), never reused; the approver is still an enabled account with an approver role, the same person, none of the authors, and no enabled admin account is that person (I17); the version widens no role held by any enabled account of the approver's person; no account decision waits for qa; the recomputed diff is byte for byte the one approved; the version passes the checker. It prints the diff summary (each changed target, hosts' admitted roles before → after, what each role gains or loses), runs the ten artefact checks as a baseline (eight before Superset stage C added Superset roles, nine before research Phase 2b added Research network policies; any FAIL refuses: fix it first), asks [y/N], reads Keycloak and the version again, then commits the version with its grants compiled from it in one transaction, rewrites the host file, runs every scoped mode and the ten checks again. --check-only stops before the question and writes nothing.yes
--rollback-to <K> --by <username> --reason "<text>" [--check-only]Since slice 4.5. Restores superseded version K (confirmed by qa, not disputed; a change or skeleton version with its approval evidence) as a new version of kind rollback, applied at once and confirmed afterwards by a qa person other than you in the Access Policy. Refused when K's rows under today's skeleton would give any role more than K was approved for ("draft from version K in the Policy UI … and have qa approve it"); rows naming a group or role the skeleton retired are dropped and counted. An open change or skeleton version is withdrawn; pending account decisions are listed, not refused; a check already failing is reported and never drives a revert. Asks you to type yes.yes
--audit <N>Since slice 4.5. Read-only: recompiles version N with the compiler of its recorded commit from its rows, runs the checker, verifies its approval token against the key recorded at apply, and compares every artefact digest with its applied record (cli.py audit-version); exit 1 on a mismatch, 2 when the record cannot be reproduced (for example a commit no longer in the repository).no

--by is your Keycloak username in the realm: it is recorded as the person who applied the version (a claim), and a qa person other than you confirms the version in the Policy UI once it exists (IAM 4.3). Exit codes: 0 done; 1 refused or failed, nothing changed, or (since 4.5) a failed rollout fully reverted; 2 a usage error or a precondition (the bootstrap waits: no migration 008c, Keycloak down, an unknown --by; for N also a check already failing, a narrowing git skeleton, a commit that cannot be reproduced); 3 committed but not finished: run --resume (never for --propose-skeleton or --withdraw-open, after whose commit nothing follows); 130 interrupted before the commit, nothing changed.

When the rollout fails (since 4.5). After the commit every scoped mode runs, then the ten checks; a failed command (or a check FAILing that did not FAIL in the baseline) is retried with every later one, up to 3 attempts 20 s apart. After ./deploy-infra.sh --policy-only apply.sh waits up to 150 s until every Ready pod of the services that check routes reads the new route table; access-api may answer 503 to account decisions for about a minute after the commit when the version moves a role's widening (the summary says so). A change or rollback version still failing after the third attempt is reverted: a second transaction puts the previous version back and files partial_apply {reverting} under it, its artefacts are re-rendered, then partial_apply {reverted} is recorded under N (approved again) and applied {reverted_from} under the previous version; exit 1, "Fix the cause and run … again".
